Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Considering that unemployment remains at 8.6 per cent for the third month in a row, clearly demonstrating that there has been no improvement in the Canadian economy, and considering that the real unemployment rate for young people in Canada has jumped alarmingly to 19.4 per cent, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.
Today the newspaper Le Devoir refers to two reports of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights about cases involving serious violations of human rights in Paraguay and Uruguay. The report mentions "sexual tortures on political prisoners." As for Paraguay, the report points out that:
During the siege, several individuals died in mysterious circumstances. Hundreds of people of all political leanings have been arrested without any charge being laid against them nor any judgment delivered. The Catholic Church and other religious organizations have been persecuted, etc.
As a result of those serious violations of human rights, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the House severely blame the Paraguay and Uruguay authorities for serious violations of human rights as quoted in the ICHR report and ask that those two states allow the ICHR to investigate on the spot.

subsubtopic: TRIPARTITE MEETING ON GRAIN SHIPMENTS-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I would like to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. There is a massive backlog of grain shipments that has developed this spring whereby Canada is at least 1.2 million tons behind schedule, an amount that represents one full month of grain delivery to our ports. Since the demurrage charges paid by the western farmer are mounting daily and are projected to total $30 million by July 31, the end of the current crop year, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave):
That the Prime Minister chair a meeting with top officials of the Canadian Wheat Board, and senior management of the railways, and port authorities, in order to try to resolve the disaster threatening western grain shipments. This emergency meeting should be held as soon as humanly possible.

During the past five years the Liberal federal government has allowed the youth unemployment problem to get totally out of control. The government has blamed the problem on world economic problems, the baby boom, the increase in the participation rate-

Mr. Speaker, with today's tragic unemployment figures showing that our unemployment has jumped 119,000 in the year, 14,000 in the last month, and with 27 per cent of our youth who do not plan to go back to school on the jobless list at the present time, would the Minister of Finance indicate to the House what has gone wrong with his tax credits that he told us would give stimulus to the economy in January and February? What has gone wrong with his employment credit program to create jobs in this country?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the hon. member that he forgot to mention that there were 300,000 more people working this May than there were last May. Of course the increase in the participation rate is still a difficult problem to cope with. I
June 13, 1978

would just remind hon. members that in the last year we have created a lot more jobs, and that the measures which we put forward in the budget of April 10 will take some time to find their way into the Canadian economy. The performance of our economy is just as good as any other country's in the western world with the exception of Japan.

Surely the minister must agree that the greatest challenge we have in this country is that of getting people back to work. The minister says our record is good. Would he tell the Elouse if, as we have suggested repeatedly, he has done a study to determine how the United States has been able to keep its unemployment level down to 6.1 per cent compared to our 8.6 per cent, bearing in mind that if we had the same rate in this country a quarter of a million people would be working today who are not presently working due to the policies of this government?

Mr. Speaker, the increase in the labour force in Canada is double that of the United States, and we have created 300,000 new jobs since last year. I think that is a commendable performance, although there is still room for improvement. The growth of the labour force far exceeds that of other countries and with our expansionist policies we continue to encourage growth in Canada. That is why hon. members sometimes complain of the current level of budgetary deficit of the government, but that policy is aimed at stimulating the Canadian economy.

I have a final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Apparently the Minister of Finance cannot see the strained situation in this country, of high deficits and high unemployment at the same time. If the minister has not done a study generally with respect to how the United States brought its unemployment levels down, has he at least done what we have suggested also, and that is make a study of the New England states to see how they have been able to get their unemployment levels down to almost half our level, bearing in mind that Newfoundland now has unemployment of over 17 per cent, that there is 13 per cent unemployment throughout the Atlantic provinces, and 11.5 per cent in Quebec?

Mr. Speaker, I know there is a special problem in the east. It is a traditional problem. The Department of Manpower and Immigration has some job creation programs that are directed to the level of unemployment in those parts of the nation. We are following some very aggressive policies on fisheries development which I think will find some long term benefits for that part of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address my question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. As of May 31 all funding ceased to the one program offered by the federal government which was helping to provide useful permanent jobs, that program being the year-round JET program. When the minister replied to a question I put on March 14 this year he stated:
... I am particulary impressed with the job experience training program which has resulted in an increase from 1,000 to 14,000 young people participating. It is a good program.
Did the minister know the program would be discontinued eleven weeks after he made that statement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: DISCONTINUANCE OF JOB EXPERIENCE TRAINING PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is nice to see the conversion of the hon. member. I indicated to him what an excellent program it was, and he poured nothing but scorn on it. When we decided to change the emphasis of that program and move it into the tax credit program, all of a sudden it is a wonderful, brilliant program. It was that before. It was while it was being implemented, and it is a program of which we can be proud. It took the lead for things like the employment tax program. Does he feel this is an effective way of helping youth unemployment?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
Since the Ontario premier would not allow the French language rights bill to be passed, although it had the almost unanimous support of the Ontario legislature, and considering the negative impact that this action will have on Canadian unity and the respect of the fundamental rights of French Canadians, could the Prime Minister tell us whether he intends to make representations to the Ontario premier so that he will at last do justice to the French Canadians in his province?

GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO CURB UNEMPLOYMENT IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister with regard to a problem which affects the province of Quebec more specifically.
According to a recent study, it has been proved that from August 1977 to April 1978, the rate of unemployment which, among men of 35 to 44 years of age was 3.9 per cent and among those of 45 to 54, was 3.8 per cent, rose to 9.2 per cent or 9.3 per cent which represents an increase of 116 per cent to 128 per cent. As the Minister of Finance is supposed to meet his provincial counterparts in the near future, would he be willing to assure us that he will put on his agenda proposals to help that category of people?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO CURB UNEMPLOYMENT IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at that meeting, we will have a look at all economic policies throughout the land, and in each one of the provinces. Naturally, I, too, am sorry to see that since November 1976 the Quebec economy has been ailing increasingly.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO CURB UNEMPLOYMENT IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance.
It is a fact that according to this study, this phenomenon would be attributable to the structural weakness of the manufacturing sector, emphasizing that 55,000 jobs have been lost in Quebec over the past three years. 1 am sure the minister will understand that all this happened before the election of the current government. Under these circumstances, would the Minister of Finance agree to make concrete proposals to his provincial counterparts concerning especially the manufacturing sector?

Also, Mr. Speaker, we have made very extensive efforts in the case of Canadair, a corporation which was about to close, where we increased the number of jobs from 1,200 to 4,800. 1 should like to indicate that in connection with this project, the Quebec government had refused to co-operate with the federal government's efforts to improve the situation.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It has to do with the Peter Treu case. Anyone reading the report this morning by George Bain in the Gazette must conclude that justice was not done and that the accused was denied the rights to which every accused should be entitled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman refers to an article in this morning's Gazette which I have not seen, and therefore I cannot base my reply on that. As far as I know that evidence is secret, and 1 do not see how the right hon. gentleman could have access to it any more than 1 could. The judgment itself is secret, but as the right hon. gentleman knows, the Minister of

Justice has made an application-which, I understand, will be heard Friday-for the publication of that judgment. It is his belief and our hope that after having read the judgment perhaps a little more light will be shone on this case.

Wrong.

-and that therefore both parties agreed to this procedure.
We also know that the case is being appealed, and the right hon. gentleman knows that, if justice is to be done, the usual way for litigants to obtain justice is to appeal to a higher court and not to jump from the judicial system to the legislative or parliamentary system, as the right hon. gentleman is suggesting.

Mr. Speaker, that is interesting, but it is the right of the Government of Canada to grant a new trial when every vestige of reasonable conduct is set aside during a trial. Except for the sentencing, which took place in open court, all of the trial was conducted in secret. Even the judgment is not available to be seen. Witnesses were sworn to secrecy and were not allowed to hear other witnesses.
One witness, a United States air force officer, has been bound to an undertaking not to talk about the Treu case since 1975. There is no justice in that kind of conduct, and I appeal to the Prime Minister to ensure that justice is in fact done by ordering a new trial. Appeal courts will not be able to determine that any of these things were of such a nature as to deny a fair trial.
Anyone outside the legal circumference can come to no other conclusion than that what was done in this case was a disgraceful travesty of justice.

Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman is suggesting that the federal government interfere with the judicial process. If we were to do that, he would be the first to cry indignantly that that should not be done.
A case begins before a magistrate in a province. Magistrates are not even appointed by the federal government. This case comes under a law which is a law of this parliament but which has not been changed since the right hon. gentleman was Prime Minister, so the issue is not a matter of taking issue with the law which the right hon. gentleman himself knew about when he was Prime Minister. He is taking issue with a process before a court which is not under our jurisdiction, and between parties who did not ask our advice on how to proceed but who accepted a procedure and who have now gone to appeal.
The right hon. gentleman is suggesting that the government of the day intervene in this process, say we do not trust courts of appeal, and tell them what to do. That is absolute nonsense.

Order, please. On May 8 last, the hon member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) rose on a question of privilege. According to his question of privilege, 1 believe that he considered that the coverage of the leadership convention of the Social Credit party held in Winnipeg on May 7, 1978, was inadequate. On May 11, 1978, the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) gave his reply. 1 have taken under consideration the complaint of the hon. member for Bellechasse, the reply of the hon. Secretary of State as well as the precedents concerning parliamentary privileges. The definition of parliamentary privilege is well known to hon. members, and I shall repeat it in English-
June 13, 1978

Parliamentary privilege is the sun of the peculiar rights enjoyed by each House collectively as a constituent part of the High Court of Parliament, and by members of each House individually, without which they could not discharge their functions, and which exceed those possessed by other bodies or individuals. Thus privilege, though part of the law of the land, is to a certain extent an exemption from the ordinary law.

Therefore, parliamentary privilege is extended collectively to the House and individually to the hon, members. It does not extend to the political party as such, and it does not go much further than the right of the House to obtain the services of members of the House and the right of hon. members to freedom of speech in this House. It goes without saying that I fully appreciate the difficulty raised by the hon. member for Bellechasse, which is essentially a grievance. It is unfortunate that our procedure does not provide hon. members more opportunities to express grievances and obtain direct answers.
It is therefore impossible for me to consider this matter in the context of parliamentary privilege and I can only suggest to the hon. member for Bellechasse that he pursue this affair by other means, perhaps before the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, which is now considering the estimates of the Secretary of State.

However, one of the basic difficulties we are encountering increasingly here is in respect of questions posed directly to ministers. 1 know that no minister is under any obligation whatsoever to answer a question, but 1 would think that at least it should be the tradition of this House, since this tradition seems to be more honoured by breach than by observance, that it should now be part of the rules that there should be some inhibition, if not prohibition, on ministers giving lengthy answers that in no way respond to the questions posed.
In two instances this afternoon in respect of the exercise of jurisdiction by the minister responsible for the status of women and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), I asked specific questions about actions that might be taken under their jurisdictions, given the serious situation with regard to unemployment of women today. Mr. Speaker, I rise on what I consider to be a very serious question of privilege. On June 1 I raised in this House the question of the possibility of a clear conflict of interest involving the situation of a former minister of finance, the same man who was former minister of national defence, in taking a position, so soon after he exercised these particular government responsibilities, with the MacDonnell-Douglas Corporation.
My concern at that time was that the minister, having had such major responsibilities in the government as finance and defence, should have exercised more discretion in terms of time in moving to a corporation which was in itself involved in serious negotiations and contract proposals involving millions of dollars with the federal government.
I have been disturbed subsequent to that time, June 1, by further developments involving the government, which by no means eradicate my concern about the possibilities of political interference in contracting procedures of the federal government. According to minutes of a meeting that took place in 1975, involving the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), who was then the minister of state for urban affairs, it is stated, and I quote from those minutes:
The minister wants to make sure the firms chosen for major contracts... are cleared politically with the ministers responsible, through his office.
This matter was appropriately raised in the House yesterday by a member of the Conservative party in the form of a question. When that particular matter was raised in a responsible fashion in the form of a question, I had hoped the minister, in this case the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), who dealt with it would have taken the opportunity of removing any possibility that there was political interference in the

June 13, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Broadbenl
awarding of major contracts in government financial operations.
Quite the contrary took place. Not only did the minister not say that this was not the practice in 1975, he went on to say, and I quote from Hansard from yesterday at page 6277:
-I do not see anything wrong with that statement.
What are the implications of this? It would seem to me that the implication is that for a major contract-and God knows what happens if the contract is just a minor one-the normal competitive tendering processes are being ignored. I hope the minister will take the time to clarify this situation.
If it is normal to get political clearance, then it is normal by logical processes to conclude that the normal competitive tendering procedures are being abrogated in some way. This is why we have to be concerned about this matter. As I understand it, the normal contracting procedures do allow for some ministerial discretion. The company with the lowest bid does not automatically get the contract, and that makes sense; there are good arguments which can be made in support of that. For example, the firm with the lowest bid may not be a reliable supplier. For other reasons in the consideration and the view of the ministry the company may not have the capacity to deliver on time or in kind. There could be other technical considerations that would cause a responsible minister not to accept the lowest bid.
However, the implication of the minute of 1975, to which I referred earlier, and the answer given yesterday in the House by the Minister of Finance, is that among the considerations that pertain to major contracts is the political reliability of the company concerned. How is that to be defined? Is it a bonus by that company to the Liberal Party of Canada? Is it to be defined as a company that normally helps out the Liberal party of Canada, if not in a direct financial way, by some other means? It seems to me that political reliability cannot mean anything else other than one of these two possibilities. I submit that either one of them is contrary to the public interest.
I thought that it had been taken for granted some time ago in the procedures of this parliament that major contracts are to be resolved entirely on non-political considerations. I was deeply disturbed when I read that original minute of 1975 where it said political considerations were going to come into play, and I was even more disturbed yesterday in the House when 1 heard the Minister of Finance, who had the opportunity to deny the practice, in fact confirm it, saying that he could see nothing wrong with the statement.
My question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, is very straightforward, and I can rely on a prima facie case. I would think that the people of Canada would be scandalized by the implications, unless this matter is cleared up irrevocably today. Canadians expect the Government of Canada to have honest, clear-cut, non-political dealings with corporations involving public funds. If that is not the case, then it reflects unfavourably on all members of this House. All members of parliament
[Mr. Broadbent.l
are implicated when there is a serious wrongdoing by the government, if that is what is involved.
If you rule, Mr. Speaker, after we hear from others who may want to participate in this question of privilege, that I have a prima facie case, I will move that the matter be referred to the committee on privileges and elections.

Mr. Speaker, I think this matter deserves an explanation even though it is not a proper question of privilege. With regard to the questions asked yesterday by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), he referred to the fact that a minister wished to be informed as to what was going on in his region. There is the obligation that every minister follow the rules as set out by the Treasury Board, which state that all contracts are awarded to the lowest bidder. If it is not the lowest bidder that gets the contract, then it has to be approved by the Treasury Board, and there must be valid reasons as to why the lowest bidder did not get the contract. This has happened, of course.
What the hon. member was referring to, however, perhaps needs clarification. It is absolutely normal that ministers would want to be made aware of what is happening within their regions. It is extremely important because among the responsibilities of the ministers in cabinet is that they make sure that what is done by this government is made well known to the people.
There is no inference that the normal way of proceeding is to interfere with the allocation of contracts. The rules and regulations are well known. They are established by the Treasury Board and all contracts have to be approved according to the practices. When they say that matters should be referred to the regional ministers, it is just normal practice because the minister coming from one part of Canada or another has a role as a minister to make sure that the activities of the federal government in that area are knwon to him in order that he can explain it to the public. This is not interference into the due process of the allocation of contracts. That is what I meant.
It is very normal that a minister representing a region would want to be informed, and he is certainly entitled to know if there is a contract being allowed within his jurisdiction. In no way did I intend to lead the House to believe yesterday that a minister has the right to intervene in the allocation of contracts. It is just not the practice because the rules and regulations are well known. Every contract must go to the lowest
June 13, 1978

bidder unless there is a valid reason not to do so. When it is allocated, it is allocated by the Treasury Board and not by the minister himself.
There is nothing in there about its being regional.

I just wanted to say that that was the context of my comments in the House yesterday. If a minister seeks to be informed of what is going on in his province, it is not intervention in the due process of the allocation of contracts. This is not a question of privilege; it is merely a political point.

speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: FEDERAL COURT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO PERMIT EXAMINATION OF CONFIDENTIAL DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is designed to repeal section 42(2) of the Federal Court Act. That act provides that a minister of the Crown may, by means of filing an affidavit, absolutely debar production of any document disclosure of which he thinks may be injurious to international relations, national defence or security, federal-provincial relations or disclosing a confidence of the Privy Council. The repeal would mean that a court might examine the document and order its production if the court saw fit.
An important principle is involved in this bill. If it is passed, a minister cannot allege or put forward an absolute power to keep a document secret from the scrutiny of the courts in cases where the court says it wishes to see the document to assure itself whether the affidavit is properly filed and whether the exemptions to which it refers in fact exist, instead of leaving it to the minister to judge his own case.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

Mr. Speaker, I have been sitting in the House for ten years and we have seen a few motions such as the one introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) today. We have even discussed in the House the passage of that famous Standing Order 75C enabling a minister to restrict unilaterally the debate as the Minister of Finance is doing today.
Mr. Speaker, we are constantly before the following dilemma between the government and the opposition, that is the government wants to pass bills quickly while the Opposition wants to consider them in depth to gather all the information

before the question is put. As a result of that dilemma, the government is always inclined to conclude the debate quickly. It happens sometimes that the debates are too long, but in the present case, 1 would like to point out that the minister is presuming that the debates will be dragging. That is a cavalier and arrogant way of measuring the value of the debate and contributions of members of this House. That bill was not even discussed properly considering that already it has somehow come up against opposition on second reading and then in this debate in committee, well, no sooner had we begun this debate that the minister already anticipated that it would be too long and he had to limit it. That is in my opinion, an entirely abnormal way of holding up the rights of this House.
Mr. Speaker, like other members who spoke before me, I must object categorically to that. Indeed, I believe that if you finally reach the conclusion that a new rule will be established in this House, the debates will automatically be limited as soon as the issue being considered is controversial. Well, Mr. Speaker, a regime applying such principles is a dictatorial regime. So I do not believe that this government should be allowed to get into that. So, Mr. Speaker, as I said, I am most strongly opposed to that, particularly as an independent member of this House, being accountable only to the voters of my riding, who have the right like anyone else to know the opinion of their representative in this House, perhaps even more than other members, I must categorically object to that decision.
The minister, the Prime Minister and the whole government have already become so tied up in a way that I would describe as stupid in this debate and the fact the minister should continue to want to breach our rights in another way leaves the impression that he thinks he is condoning the ill-intentioned and clumsy moves he made by cutting down this debate. As other members have suggested before me, the minister regrets what he did and no longer wants to hear about the solution he proposed.
We are not in this House to cover up the mistake made by a government or by a particular minister. That is why I do not believe they are justified in breaching the rights and privileges of members of this House simply because a minister messed things up. Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks at this stage. This will be the only opportunity I shall have to participate because I shall be leaving later today for parliamentary business outside Canada.
On listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) it occurred to me we should do some hard thinking as to why there was not the same unanimity on this
June 13, 1978

bill as there was with regard to the veterans legislation to which he referred. Mr. Speaker, the day of the traditional budget has gone. The days when the minister could call in his advisers and prepare appropriate tax and fiscal measures in great secrecy and then introduce them with a flourish in a dramatic way are probably gone for ever. There are many reasons for this, not the least of which is the new economic situation in which we find ourselves, the continuance of inflation at a time when unemployment is so high. We look to those in the academic community for guidance in these matters but there is no Lord Keynes on the scene today.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has a difficult task. He has to devise a new type of budget in new circumstances. For one thing, combined municipal and provincial expenditure substantially exceeds that of the federal authority, as has been the case for some years. The state of the economy in the various regions of the country is, moreover, so diverse that it is no longer possible to take a uniform course as dictated by the wisdom of the minister of finance and the mandarins in Ottawa. This implies discussion with provincial spokesmen and, of course, abandonment of the traditional approach to the budget which was one of complete secrecy since, in the process of consultation, there is bound to be some sacrifice of that principle.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance for his innovative approach. He travelled. He consulted with provincial ministers. He sought ideas. The approach he took to the previous budget was based on personal income tax cuts and corporate tax concessions which failed to stimulate the economy. It did not work. Mr. McKeough of Ontario suggested there ought to be a cut in sales tax. That was a suggestion which came from a member of a government of a different political complexion but was adopted as the essence of the solution found by the Minister of Finance in his search for a new approach.
Eight of the provinces agreed with that approach. No sales tax existed in Alberta. A different deal was struck with the maritimes which, as we all know, had special problems. The minister thought a consensus had been reached. But Quebec held out. Then, after the budget had been announced, a game was played in hindsight by the spokesmen for Quebec. It was not played in good faith because whatever the federal government did there would be an attempt at political one-upmanship.
Any concerned Canadian who is worried about the management of our economy knows we cannot rely on the traditional fiscal and monetary tools to do the job in the way it has been approached in the past. Innovation has proved to be a difficult procedure. Nevertheless, those responsible for the attempt to denigrate the preparation of a budget by a new process will have to answer to the voters and to the people generally. I support the budget because it is the first of a new type which the situation demands. Today a minister of finance must innovate. He must be flexible and the measures he takes must respond to the needs of different parts of the country.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, in effect, that if we can all agree on something we can put it through quickly-we do not even need to debate it. The point is that we do not agree. Even the analysis of the subject matter is open to disagreement among prominent people both in the academic and in the business world. As I say, today a minister of finance has to innovate, but whenever there is innovation there is bound to be a difference of opinion.
Opposition spokesmen complain that we have spent only a short while on this stage of the bill. Of course, it means nothing to them that we have already spent six days discussing the budget itself and another 11 days on second reading, or that debate at that stage was brought to an end only by a time allocation order. I noted that when the minister gave notice of a time allocation order yesterday with respect to the committee stage there was a sudden change of heart and things moved along a little faster. But I for one am standing up and saying I support the new approach. I support the innovation.
I look forward to more innovation in future budgets and to new attempts to do things based on consultation and respect for regional differences and problems. This bill has to pass. We cannot debate until the end of time. We cannot go through the sophistry of saying that there have been six days for the budget, 11 days for something else and a day for tariff resolutions but that that is all irrelevant and that we have to work on all these clauses and spend all the time we have. No legislative body can afford that luxury. Let us get on with the job.

Mr. Chairman, as the explanatory note to this clause states that it is designed to correct an error relating to the application of subsection 85(7) as amended by chapter 1 of the statutes for the current session, could the minister tell us what the error is that they have made here and why we are being called upon to correct it?

Mr. Chairman, as usual, I will read the technical explanation. This is a relieving technical amendment bringing into force the provision of last year's tax legislation, being Bill C-l 1. Section 85 of the act provides a roll-over that is a mechanism for the deferral of tax that will otherwise arise on certain transfers of property to a Canadian corporation. In order to qualify for this roll-over an election must be filed by the due date of the tax return for the year of transfer.
In a number of situations, taxpayers failed to Tile the required election on time. Subsection 85(7) was amended in Bill C-l 1 to permit the filing of an election within three years from the normal due date. The amendment in Bill C-ll was made applicable to transfers of property made in 1975 and subsequent taxation years. The Bill C-ll amendment should have been effected before an election normally due after May 6, 1974. This change simply corrects the coming into force accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, could the minister confirm that this is one of the amendments that he hoped to make in the committee of the whole stage with respect to Bill C-l 1 but got caught in his own closure mechanism and was not able to make the amendment at that time?

Mr. Chairman, it was an amendment that I wanted to put forward in the debate, but because there was a lot of foot dragging in second reading, we did not have the time to proceed normally clause by clause and we had to limit the debate, I believe, after five weeks. This amendment, which would delete a reference to the Northwest Territories as not being a province for the purpose of section 120, together with the amendment to subsection 124(1) proposed in clause 31, would implement paragraph (12) of the income tax motion, which read as follows:-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is nice to see you.

The inappropriate remark from the hon. member does not call for any comments. I would simply say that if he had read the act, he would readily understand that

this is a very positive measure designed to allow the Northwest Territories to reach a more autonomous status than they had before. This is in line with the policy established by this government when I was Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development with a view to transferring to the northern council more power than it had under the governments which were in power before the Liberals came in. Regarding this amendment, Mr. Chairman, I will read the general comment as I have done for the other clauses, and I quote:
Since January 1, 1978 the Northwest Territories have their own income tax system and have since concluded a tax collection agreement with the government of Canada.
The amendment proposed to the definition of the term "province" contained in paragraph 120(4)(b) of the act results from the Northwest Territories being granted the status of a province for the purposes for the Income Tax Act. Before January 1, 1978 residents of the Northwest Territories had to pay a federal income tax of 43 per cent under section 120(1) of the act. Residents of the Yukon remain subject to this additional federal income tax. The amount of income tax payable by Northwest Territories residents for fiscal year 1978 and subsequent years will not be modified by this change because the additional tax which they would otherwise have had to pay to the federal government will be paid to the Northwest Territories government.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to the Northwest Territories I would like to ask the minister if he can tell us the approximate rate of taxation to which the taxpayers of these territories will now be subjected? Is it based on an average of the federal income tax and that of the various provinces? Is it rather calculated on the basis of the tax in Alberta or Ontario? And with regard to the Yukon which as a territory has not yet availed itself of the powers granted to it on January 1, 1978, what will be the rate of taxation for the taxpayers of that region?

Mr. Chairman, the bill does not provide for any change in the amount of tax paid by the people from the Northwest Territories at this time. They will pay the same income tax as their neighbours from the Yukon, and we will not change in any way the amount of income tax paid by the people from the Northwest Territories, but we will change the process through which the government of the Northwest Territories will be able in the future to increase or reduce income tax within its budgetary authority. Of course, there is a collection agreement with the federal government, but through this bill we are giving the government of the Northwest Territories the authority to pass legislation pertaining to income tax.

Why is the Yukon not included? Perhaps at that time the Yukon council did not request it, but since the minister told us a moment ago, when he explained the reason for this amendment, that this would affect that Yukon and the Northwest Territories which have, since January 1, 1978, a power of taxation, that is why I was wondering-I think I did hear the minister say so-under what authority a territory had the rights of a province to levy that kind of tax.

In other words, is he empowered to disregard clause 2 amending section 122.1(2) which stipulates that where no fiscal agreement exists between the federal government and the provinces, there is an $85 reimbursement? Can he disregard that provision and refer instead to clause 1 which provides for a $100 reimbursement merely by changing the schedule?

Legally, Mr. Chairman, we have a choice, once clauses 30(a) and (6) have been passed, to add the province of Quebec to the schedule to part 1 of the act. However, the government has decided to proceed as the bill stipulated as introduced, that is by reimbursing immediately $40 million to the Quebec government, and reimbursing to the Quebec taxpayers an amount of up to $85 as provided for in this bill. Naturally, as we know, Mr. Chairman, 1 made proposals to the Quebec government exactly two weeks ago with a view to coming to an agreement, and if the Quebec government had accepted my proposal on that Wednesday, we could have included Quebec in the first schedule, and payments could have been made in the spring of 1979. But, in the reply 1 received from Mr. Parizeau one week later, he told me that, as the formula advocated by the second part of clause 30 was public knowledge, he had no objections to it and advised me that he would, one way or the other, take steps to recover those amounts of money, which it is in his power and his duty to do if he has budgetary problems and has to increase his taxes; and I have no business interfering in that field.
Income Tax Act
The second proposal he made in his letter would lead to amendments in clauses 30(a) and 30(b). That, of course, would involve interest payments and a substantial change in clause 30. Since I gather, from his letter, that he would be satisfied if we adopted clause 30(6) concerning Quebec, I did not think it appropriate to choose the other alternative as this would result in major changes and administrative complexities. So I shall opt for the formula which seems acceptable to the Quebec government. I had myself suggested that Quebec be included in clause 30(a), but that was rejected by Mr. Parizeau who wanted a cash payment of $40 million, which was impossible under 30(a). That is why 30(6) seems acceptable to Mr. Parizeau, and the government has decided to go that route.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. Hon. members will recall that the Speaker ruled that this clause could not be dealt with until we had a proper ways and means motion concurred in by the House. Was the ways and means motion tabled by the minister concurred in?
The motion was concurred in yesterday afternoon.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We are informed by the Minister of Finance that the motion was concurred in yesterday afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, I merely wanted to ask the minister to clarify the statement he made. I may be incorrect but my understanding is that Mr. Jacques Parizeau, the minister of finance of the province of Quebec, had asked for $40 million as part of the settlement, and that the balance, the $186 million, could be paid on either basis, either by an $85 rebate on this year's tax or by a rebate of $100 for 1978.
The minister says that there is some administrative difficulty. I would have thought the opposite would be true, that it would be much better if all the provinces were on the same basis, namely that this reduction would be for the 1978 tax year and would be for $100. The government has always been strong in saying that it does not want any special status for any province, it wants them all to be treated alike. If it is correct that Mr. Parizeau said that he does not care which of the options the federal government selects, I cannot understand why the Minister of Finance has not selected the one which would have had uniform application to all the provinces and removed a good deal of the irritation that has been generated during this debate.
6364

June 13, 1978
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, in Mr. Parizeau's letter, what is called his option two, he is asking for $40 million right away and $85 for those taxpayers on the list for 1978, but to be deducted from the income tax of the Quebec taxpayers only in the spring at the time of filing. That is why in his request there is something different from the other provinces. The week before I offered to deduct $100 in the spring of 1979, but he rejected that proposition. He wanted $40 million cash and $85 in the spring. As we wanted to make the federal contribution of the money left over-because there was no agreement on the $186 million-not to penalize Quebeckers but because there was no agreement between the governments we decided to proceed with the $85 payment right away.
There are a lot of people who do not know why we have to proceed that way. As the hon. member knows, 1 believe it was at the time when he was premier of Saskatchewan that Mr. Duplessis decided to have his own tax collection system and that is why we have to operate in a different fashion. It is not due to any action by the federal government. For Saskatchewan, Ontario and Manitoba on budget night the federal government reduced the income tax by $100, and those ministers of finance a week later raised their income tax by $100, and agreed to my plan to reduce sales tax.
In the case of the province of Quebec there was no such agreement. There has been no tax collection agreement with Quebec since 1954. That is why we have to rebate the money to the Quebec taxpayers directly. If the provincial governments want to collect any part of it or all of it, or even more than it, it is within their own power to do so. It is always their privilege and option to do whatever they want with their own tax, just as the federal government does with federal tax.
If Mr. Parizeau had agreed to what I offered two weeks ago, namely to have Quebec included in option one, I would have been willing to do this and it would have been exactly as with the other provinces regarding clause 38. But he does not want that. Mr. Parizeau wants $40 million cash because he has qualified partially to participate in the national program. As for the rest, I am just following the government's intentions at the time of tabling the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Before recognizing the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands on a point of order raised previously by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, if we refer to the Votes and Proceedings for Monday, June 12, at page 858 in the fourth paragraph, the motion reads:
The order being read for the consideration of a ways and means motion to amend the Income Tax Act (Sessional Paper No. 303-1/308D), laid upon the table, Thursday, June 8, 1978;
Mr. Chretien, seconded by Mr. Cullen, moved,-That the motion be concurred in.
And the question being put on the motion, it was agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, this is not the first time the minister has tried to explain this situation by virtue of the fact that Quebec is the only

province which does not have a tax collection agreement with the federal government. 1 know they have not got that. In fact, I was at the conference when Mr. Duplessis announced they would not continue the tax collection agreement with the federal government. However, I do not follow the logic of the minister as to why that needs to make any difference.
If the federal government made it clear that when people submit their 1978 income tax returns next spring they will be allowed a $100 deduction, the provincial government of Quebec could then adjust this tax as it saw fit. They could either collect that $100 or let the Quebec taxpayer have it. I see no reason why there should be two different schemes on two different bases.
A good deal of the difficulty the minister has had with this bill has been quite unnecessary. The minister several times has been very critical of the government of Quebec because he does not agree with their separatist policies. Neither do I, but I resent this intent to smear anybody who asks for fair and equal treatment for Quebec as being a separatist or as being in bed with the separatists. That is a cheap type of politics that will not get the minister or the government anywhere. It smacks of the McCarthy era. If they could not call you a communist, they said you were soft on communism, in bed with a communist or advocating what a communist would advocate if he were in your place. That does not do anything for anybody.
We have to look at this fairly. I did not get into the fight when the minister was being attacked. 1 think he has a difficult job and is doing the best he can. However, I say the minister got himself into a good deal of trouble by the hamhanded way in which this whole question of the reduction of the retail sales tax has been handled.
First, there was a finance ministers' conference and then a first ministers' conference. Those were the places where it should have been suggested to the provinces that the federal government thought that the most speedy way in which to give a stimulus to the economy was to cut the retail sales tax, and that the federal government was prepared to make some compensation in return for such action.
That was not done. The finance ministers and the premiers went home and proceeded to prepare their budgets. I ask the members of this committee to put themselves in the position of a provincial premier. After working out his budget, he has a very small surplus. He thinks he will break even and might even have enough to cover any unforeseen contingencies. He then receives a telephone call or a visit from the federal Minister of Finance who says he is prepared to pay two thirds of the cost of cutting the sales tax by three percentage points for six months, or two percentage points for nine months.
What does that mean to the provincial treasurer? It means he will be put in a deficit position. He does not want to be in a deficit position, but he cannot turn it down. What position would he be in on budget night when the Minister of Finance would say that he offered province A or province B a cut in sales tax of three percentage points and that province did not want it? What if that province turned down millions of dollars which it would have received in compensation?

June 13, 1978

The minister did not say that the provincial treasury would have had to find the money to put up the provincial share of that reduction. If given enough notice prior to making their budget, the provincial treasurer and premier could probably adjust to that. However, they cannot do it on the basis of a few days' notice. That is the reason why much of the difficulty has occurred. The minister overlooks that.
In handling the situation vis-a-vis Quebec, instead of making a cause celebre out of the situation, the Minister of Finance would have been much better to have been completely flexible. I am convinced he has done a great deal more to strengthen the hand of the Quebec government than to weaken it. Also, having two different formulae and two different tax years as a basis for paying this rebate will continue to rankle among the provinces. It was totally unnecessary. There could have been a uniform arrangement. There is no reason why the minister could not have paid the $40 million to Quebec and put them on the $100 deduction for the tax year 1978. If the minister had done that, he would have saved himself a lot of headaches.

I am pleased to hear the hon. member say that I should have consulted even more. 1 would like him to talk to his leader who, the day before the budget, got up in this House and asked me to tell the House and the nation that I had not fulfilled my obligation as the Minister of Finance to budget secrecy, that by talking to the provinces I had done away with the great British tradition of having no one know anything about the budget beforehand.
The hon. member has more experience than his leader. Perhaps he will teach him a lesson on that. I may not have had enough consultation, but it was much too much for the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. He felt I had betrayed the great British tradition of secrecy where, some years ago, the minister of finance only informed his cabinet colleagues hours before presenting his budget.
I say to the hon. member that this was not done in any rush manner. I first raised the problem at the meeting I had with the finance ministers in October. It was felt that the problem in the economy was too low a demand and that we had to stimulate that demand.
When I raised the question with them in October, there was some interest, although not much. I again raised it in the month of January. There was more interest, but no agreement. For three weeks before the budget I tried to negotiate an agreement with all the provinces. Eight were involved-Alberta with no sales tax was not involved-and they agreed to the procedure I set out to deal with this problem in a difficult situation. Everyone said yes except Mr. Parizeau of Quebec. He came along 48 hours later with a different scheme. It was too late for the other provinces to do the same because they had already introduced their own legislation.
In terms of the problem for the treasury, if there is an increase of something like 15 per cent over normal sales in the six month period, the provinces will generate enough money to cover their one third of the cost. In fact, I have heard some
Income Tax Act
reports from the treasurers of the different provinces. They are very pleased with the increased retail tax revenue following the cut. They only have to pay one third of the cut, and there has been a 15 tc 20 per cent increase. The added revenue they receive will certainly compensate for their losses.
I have done my best. I am the first to say that the mechanism is not perfect. I have tried to involve the provinces for the first time in history in attempting to develop an economic policy that makes sense for everybody. Some say that I went a bit too far. Others have told me that I was naive not to force everyone to sign an agreement before the night of the budget.
It was not, in my judgment, naivete. It was-
Incompetence.
Having regard to the hon. member's great success in banking, he would be well advised to shut up.
Go on. Tell us about it. Tell us about the banking.

I considered the separatist minister of finance from Quebec not as a separatist but as a minister of finance who was there to do what was best along with the ministers from the other provinces to stimulate the Canadian economy. Some say I should have forecast that he wanted to throw a wrench into the gears of a good federal scheme, but I do not apologise for treating him as a normal minister of finance. If I had got up in this chamber on the night of the budget and said: "I am sorry, I did not try because I could not trust the Quebec government since they do not share the same goal of a prosperous Canada as we do", everyone would have laughed at me and said: "Chretien, you are wrong; you should have treated all the ministers of finance equally".
What I want to say is this: I have tried to do something that no Minister of Finance has tried to do before. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands will recognize that as being the case. Never before has the federal Minister of Finance gone to Saskatchewan to discuss a federal budget before introducing it into the House. At the time the hon. member was premier, if I am not mistaken, cabinet ministers were informed what was in the budget on the day of the budget. So I think I have come a long way from a tradition which, in my judgment, no longer makes much sense as long as speculation in the marketplace is avoided.
I believe there should be more consultation. Indeed, it is my opinion that some of these matters should be referred to a committee of the House so that an input might be made not only by the very good advisers we have within the department but by the House of Commons on certain specific questions. I have already made a reference this year of commodity tax problems to a committee of this House so that the subject can be examined and recommendations made. I do not know whether I shall accept them or not but I should like to have input from both sides of the House before I make up my mind. The process is not easy, because if the public are allowed to
8004 5-36*72

June 13, 1978
Income Tax Act
know too much about what one is thinking there is a risk of speculation which could lead to major difficulties. Any attempt to combine the British tradition of secrecy of the budget with, if 1 might use the phrase, participatory democracy involves some risk, but I have taken many risks since I became Minister of Finance and I am willing to take that one too.
To return to the Quebec situation, if Mr. Parizeau had replied to me by saying that my proposition of two weeks ago to the effect that a $100 deduction based on the Quebec taxpayer list of 1978 was acceptable, and would have confirmed the Quebec situation to the others, I would have been pleased. But one of the problems is that although the flow of money is going into the economy of the other provinces right away, in the case of Quebec, since there is no agreement, there is $186 million which I keep in my treasury. If I want that money to go into the Quebec economy, I have to take the 1977 taxpayer list and send the taxpayers their rebate right away. Otherwise they have to wait until we have the 1978 list. That list will be available only in 1979, and so the money will not be in the Quebec economy, in theory, until the spring of next year. Since 1 was dealing with a budget intended to stimulate the economy right away, 1 think I have to move quickly. That is why 1 am proposing my present course.
There is, of course, another element, though people forget about it. Because we are dealing directly with Quebec taxpayers and not collecting the taxes for Quebec, there are some 200,000 Quebeckers who will not receive a rebate if I take the list of 1978, for the reason that since we have deducted for them $100 so far this year, in January or February or later, they will not qualify at all. It is only those who pay between $100 and $185 in taxes who will qualify. So we would have eliminated 200,000 Quebec citizens from being entitled to that credit.
I do not know what Mr. Parizeau will do. Perhaps he will decide to tax back. He has not told anybody yet. Perhaps he will consider adjusting income tax rates, perhaps he will consider adjusting the sales tax or the corporation tax. 1 do not know. I have to treat the taxpayers of Quebec on the basis of the knowlege I presently have, and on that basis, if I want the money to flow into the provincial economy and if I do not want to penalize 200,000 taxpayers in Quebec, I have to take the taxpayers list of 1977. That is the only one available to me at this time. I will then send those taxpayers a tax rabate based upon the tax they paid last year.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is worried about the 200,000 taxpayers who won't be covered if this matter is left until 1978. He is saying nothing about the hundreds of thousands of people who buy goods but will not get any rebate because they do not earn enough to pay income tax.
He said to the provinces: We want you to reduce your retail sales tax as being the fastest way to get money into circulation, to give the economy a shot in the arm. Would it not have been comparatively simple to have said instead: We will make an
estimate, which can be adjusted at the end of the fiscal year, as to what it will cost you to cut your tax either 3 per cent across the board for six months or 2 per cent across the board for nine months, or even to make selective adjustments, and we will pay you in cash 90 per cent of what our share would be, and make the adjustment at the end of the year? We may owe them some money, or they may owe us some money, but we will have paid them whatever is the federal government's share of reducing the sales tax in a lump sum that would have gone into the treasury and been available to everybody.
What the minister is now proposing is to hand money out to taxpayers, many of whom do not need it. The amount of money they are getting bears no relation whatsoever to what they have paid by way of sales tax, as compared with others who are going to get nothing although they may have paid a great deal in sales tax, being responsible for bringing up large families. I have never understood why the minister made this so complicated.
May I say one other thing to the minister. He is quite incorrect when he says my hon. friend from Oshawa-Whitby took exception to the minister's consulting the premiers. The day before the budget my hon. friend objected to the fact that the press was already reporting that aspect. He did not know the premiers were being consulted; the minister told us later they were being consulted. My hon. friend was objecting to the press being informed and to leaks of information.
We in the party have never held to any sacred tradition by virtue of which provincial governments or other agencies of government were not to be consulted before a budget was bought down. There may, it is true, be certain instances in which a person would make a killing on the stock market by having advance information about certain forms of taxes which were to be proposed, but this happens very seldom.
I do know something about the preparation of budgets, having prepared some 18 of them. Not only have I consulted with my cabinet but I have consulted with my caucus, and sometimes with my party, as well as with representatives of the municipalities through their organization. There is no need for all the traditional secrecy. I agree with the minister as to that and I am glad he is moving away from the old tradition. But he has yet to convince me that this cumbersome way of compensating for the reduction in sales tax has been justified.
I get the impression that the government has been clutching at straws. The government recognizes, as does everyone with an elementary knowledge of economic rules, that the way to get the economy moving is to put purchasing power into the pockets of people with low incomes. We all recognize that today we are not suffering from inflation. If we were suffering from inflation, we would be producing more goods. We do not have a situation in which too much money is chasing too few goods. We are not operating at more than 82 per cent of our capacity. Our problem is that the people who have money do not need any more goods so they are reinvesting it.
Those who need goods do not have the money to buy them, and therefore the minister is quite right in recognizing that we

June 13, 1978

do have to stimulate the economy. But how did the government stimulate it? It tried to do so by cutting corporation taxes. When the predecessor to the minister's predecessor, Mr. Turner, was cutting corporation taxes, we told him that corporations would not invest money-even if they had tax cuts- when they were not using the capacity they had.
Now this minister has clutched at another straw. He says he talked to the finance ministers at the finance ministers' conference-I think that was in January-and that there were discussions for a while at the first ministers' conference in February. But was any specific proposal put before them? 1 know there may have been casual reference to the fact that if retail sales taxes were cut, that would give the economy a shot in the arm; but was any specific proposal put before them? Did the federal government say it was prepared to pay the majority or part of the cost to reduce sales taxes in order to get money into circulation, particularly among low-income people? If a proposition like that were put before the first ministers or finance ministers, I think they would have accepted it; but to put it before them after they had made up their budgets and finished two conferences at which no agreement was reached really was to make their situations worse. The minister has made the situation difficult for the provinces and difficult for himself, but totally unnecessarily. I ask him specifically whether a concrete proposal was put before the finance ministers or before the first ministers when they met in January and February?

Mr. Chairman, in a way we put forward a precise proposition to the ministers of finance in October. The proposal was to reduce sales taxes by two points. I was to pay half and the provinces were to pay half. That was rejected on or about October 10, 1977.
We kept talking about it. There were discussions among officials and ministers, and we made some progress. It was not discussed at the first ministers' conference because we felt it should be dealt with at the finance ministers' level. I do not think I took anybody by surprise. The provinces were well informed six months prior to the budget that this was my priority. I was trying to get agreement.
The hon. member asks why we did not adjust cash payments to the provinces and let them have all the freedom they wanted with that money. I tried to find a way to put money into circulation without having to make a federal government expenditure. If I signed cheques amounting to $800 million, I would have been obliged to write that amount into my expenditures, and the provinces could have used that money to cut taxes. 1 know the NDP would not have objected to that approach, but many people would have considered me a big spender politician if I had added $800 million to my expenditures. I wanted to find a way which would not add to my expenditures, but which would put money into circulation. Under the scheme I am reducing my take by about $800 million and making room for the provinces so that they can raise their income taxes.
The hon. member wonders why we did not give the provinces freedom. We gave them freedom. At the beginning I told
Income Tax Act
them I wanted to cut sales taxes and we discussed how to do that. I proposed that we pay the totality of the money to the maritimes because they could not afford to participate. They do not have a manufacturing base, and they can ill afford to go into a scheme like this. Everyone agreed that that made sense.
I told Alberta that there was nothing in this scheme for Alberta. I told the Alberta finance minister that I would like to help him by cutting his sales tax. He laughed and said that Alberta has no sales tax. I told him Alberta would not be involved but that he should not be too nervous because there would be other things in the budget to please some sector of Alberta's economy. That is why there is a special provision in the budget for the heavy oil schemes which are of great interest to Alberta.
There were all kinds of suggestions made by all the other provinces as to how to cut sales taxes. We decided to call a meeting in Ottawa of the officials of all the different governments. They were to come to Ottawa for a full day. We even provided for two days if that much time would be necessary to work out the details.
Some officials said they did not want to cut their sales taxes on alcohol, cigarettes and recreation. Ontario officials said that because they had just raised those taxes. They said putting money into that area would not stimulate the economy. The officials agreed among themselves that this scheme would not apply to those three commodities. B.C. and Saskatchewan had a different problem because, being on both sides of Alberta, if they were to cut sales taxes by three points for six months there would be a lot of political pressure not to reintroduce them later on. However, they said that the two-point scheme would make more sense and would be less difficult.
I proposed that they cut their sales taxes two points for nine months rather than three points for six months. We discussed that with the other provinces. I made the same offer to the other provinces, and nobody else was interested. Now I am being asked why this was not discussed. A question was asked by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi with respect to selective sales taxes. This was not raised by Quebec at all at the time of the negotiations, so we could not forecast that Quebec wanted that. Quebec did not express its views about it or show any interest in it, so 1 could not make an offer, discuss it or call a meeting on it.
On the day of the budget Mr. Parizeau said he had no answer for me, contrary to the agreement we had. He came along 48 hours later with his special way of cutting taxes. I do not want to judge whether his scheme is good or bad; it is within his jurisdiction. He did what he wanted to do, and that is fine with me. Mr. McKeough did the same thing in Ontario two years ago with his own money. I was informed at three o'clock in the afternoon on the Wednesday following the budget that the sales tax in Quebec would be cut selectively at six o'clock that night. There was no consultation. I was informed three hours prior as to what was to be done unilaterally. The question was whether I could accept that and whether I would pay for it. I told Mr. Parizeau that that was not

June 13, 1978
Income Tax Act
part of the deal which had been agreed upon by the others and that I did not know what I would do.
Before I gave him my answer I called some other ministers of finance and told them what Quebec was doing on its own. I told them that Quebec would like to qualify for the national scheme. Three ministers of finance said that it was too late; they had already announced the scheme in their own jurisdictions. Their sales taxes had been cut since that Monday night, and it was now too late for them to make the same choice. I had given my word with regard to a procedure to all ministers of finance. I tried to get them to agree to Mr. Parizeau's scheme, but they said "no way". 1 had given my word to the ministers of finance prior to the budget. The proposition was on the table. It was agreed upon as the most sensible way to cut sales taxes.
Since there was no agreement with the other finance ministers with regard to the Quebec proposal, I could not agree. I had given my word to the ministers of finance and I evolved the scheme with them during the three weeks. Mr. Parizeau decided to go unilaterally, but under the scheme the province was qualified to receive $40 million only and we decided to pay it as a result of the tax collection agreement.
Hon. members will see that under this act there is provision for an adjustment at the end of the year. We forecast that in the reduction of income tax in Ontario, $100 will be too much for the cut in the sales tax, so that province will have to pay us back some $56 million; but in the case of British Columbia, it will not be enough and we will have to add $90 million and make an adjustment at the end of the year after verifying their books.
We did not come to an agreement with Quebec that would be acceptable to other ministers of finance; that is why we had this unpleasant confrontation. I am sorry about it; I did not provoke it, and I meant well. I even wanted to do something which was proposed by the Tory critic in a memorandun to members of his caucus in January in which he said they had to keep pressing the federal government for a scheme to cut sales tax at the retail level. This memo was read in the House by the Minister of Public Works, proposing a scheme to cut sales tax at the retail level. There were other proposals.
You mean, the federal tax.

No. I will read it later. It mentioned the federal sales tax and also the provincial tax. I know the hon. member changes his mind according to the political mood, but he concluded at that time that cutting sales tax at the retail level was the most efficient way of doing it. There was a consensus on that. That is what I tried to do. Perhaps I am imputing motives to Mr. Parizeau.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The minister has referred to a memorandun allegedly written by myself in which I said that the provincial sales tax was the

proper approach. I would like him to produce that memorandum.

I quoted what the Minister of Public Works read to the House from a text which he attributed to the hon. member for York-Simcoe. If the hon. member wishes to deny he ever wrote such a memorandum, I will accept his word and later I will produce the document.
Oh, oh!
Will you produce it?
If you did not say that, then say so.
Produce it.
I do not have the document.
You are wrong, again.

If the hon. member denies he ever wrote such a piece, let him say so. I just said I had good reason to believe that when the Minister of Public Works spoke, he spoke with some knowledge. We will find out where he got his documentation. I do not have it with me. I am just saying that in the case of Quebec, they did not want to agree to the national scheme. I said, and I repeat, that I am not surprised. In their view of Canada, any good thing that is proposed by the federal government is not in their political interests. We know what their political interests are. Their political interests are to prove that confederation has never worked, is not working now, and will never work in the future. It was in their political interests to throw a wrench into the gears of my scheme. I said they did not want to try it, but I worked in good faith and treated them as I treat any other government, as is proper so long as they are part of confederation.
What Quebec did, after eight provinces had reached agreement, was to come 48 hours later and say to us that they wanted something else. I have no choice: I will pay them $40 million and I will pay $85 to each Quebec taxpayer right away. If Mr. Parizeau wishes to collect it back in taxes, that is within his jurisdiction and he can do so. It is up to him, not me. If he wishes to incur a bigger deficit, that is his option. I am not running his shop. We are reducing the tax of the federal taxpayers in Quebec right away so that the money will be in their pockets as quickly as possible.
That is the good political way of doing it.

Mr. Chairman, I see that the hon. member for York-Simcoe wishes to speak and I will certainly not monopolize this discussion. I just want to say two things with respect to what the minister has just said.
First of all, I find it absolutely appalling that a Minister of Finance would say the reason he adopted a clumsy technique of making rebates, which is inequitable and unjust, rather than paying cash to the provincial governments for tax collection which they have forgone, is that by so doing he would have
June 13, 1978

enlarged his budget by some $800 million and would have been criticized for it. Surely, it is incomprehensible that a minister would adopt such a clumsy, unworkable and administratively difficult process.
It is not at all difficult.

The minister shakes his head. We will see before he is finished with it. I have watched rebates. I have watched the Social Credit government of Alberta making payments to every citizen who was to get a certain share of the oil revenue. Some people were paid twice, many people were not paid, and some dead people were paid. The minister has not finished with that one yet. I think it is administratively clumsy, unfair and inequitable. The only reason the minister gave for it was that if he had adopted a more simple procedure, he would have added several hundred million dollars to the budget and would have been criticized. The people of Canada would not be so naive as to criticize him if they recognized that the money was being used to enable provincial governments to reduce their sales tax for a short period of time. The minister does not have much faith in the public if he advances that as an argument: it is a very weak argument indeed.
The other point I want to make is that when the minister outlines, as he has several times, his quarrel with the government of Quebec with respect to selective sales tax cuts, he gives as his reason the fact that the other provinces were not in agreement and thought an agreement had been entered into and, therefore, Quebec should be required to make a lateral tax cut rather than a selective tax cut as they did.
1 do not think the minister has always felt it necessary to follow what the provinces have done. If the provinces had chosen to select an across-the-board tax cut, they should have been prepared to accept it. They agreed to that, and I do not see why they should have objected to a selective tax cut, because one of the values of a selective tax cut is not only that it would reduce the taxes paid by the consumer, but it would, at the same time, stimulate local industry. Certainly, if British Columbia had had the opportunity to cut taxes on building materials in order to stimulate housing, it would have had a double effect: it would have reduced the expenditures of the consumer and, at the same time, given quite a fillip to the forest products industry.
Therefore, I think the main objective the minister had in mind was to stimulate the economy, and whether a province wanted to do it by lateral tax cuts or by selective tax cuts was, it seems to me, totally irrelevant. I remind the minister that that is not the reason he gave to the House when he was debating the matter on second reading and when we were discussing changes in the ways and means motion. The minister then said that to allow any province to apply selective tax cuts was equivalent to putting up tariffs, and that was protectionism. That is sheer nonsense. It would have been protectionism if a province had said, "We will cut the tax for those things that are produced in our province, but if a product comes in from another province the sales tax will apply." That
Income Tax Act
would have been protectionism. But to remove a portion of the sales tax, or all of it, from any single commodity which would be of benefit to whatever province produced it would have been of benefit to the economy and would certainly have been of benefit to the consumer.
I am not going to belabour this any longer, but I say again to the minister that the difficulty in which he finds himself results from lack of long-term planning. Much of this difficulty could have been eliminated if the government, instead of proceeding on an ad hoc basis, trying something today and something else next week, had sat down last fall and made a concrete proposal. The minister said he made a concrete proposal, offering provinces 50 per cent of the cost of the cut in retail sales taxes. I tell him right now that if I had been representing the provinces, I would not have accepted 50 per cent compensation from the federal government. Does the minister realize that in many of the provinces, retail sales tax revenue is one of the most important items-the largest item in some of them? To ask the provinces to absorb half the cost of that reduction would be asking them to assume a burden they cannot afford. Therefore, the minister could not have expected anything else.
