Mr. Chairman, before dinner I was discussing with the minister his general reaction to the Parizeau letter of June 7. I was asking whether the minister did not feel there was a constitutional problem in the way he has persisted in handling the payment of $85 to residents of Quebec, compared to the much easier system he used with the other provinces, which was simply giving a reduction for 1978 of $85 with respect to federal tax. That would be something in which residents of Quebec could share, and in turn the Quebec government would simply take over the room given up by the federal government.
I was making the point that if the minister had co-operated in following that approach, he would have been in a similar position to that which he is now working out with the other eight provinces, which is presumably an approach that would be acceptable not only to Mr. Parizeau but to the majority of members of the National Assembly.
It makes such sweet, reasonable sense that once again 1 ask the minister why he persists in doing it the hard way, as opposed to the relatively easy way of giving a reduction of $85 to the residents of Quebec in 1978 similar to the $100 he is giving the other provinces, and let the Quebec government adjust their own tax structure to take up the $85. The two things would dovetail during 1978 and the minister would avoid the confrontation which he seems to relish with the Quebec government.

Mr. Chairman, I have explained the situation many times, but I suppose I have to repeat it. I have answered that type of question since April 12, but the hon. member still does not seem to understand. There was no agreement with Quebec to cut sales taxes. They left $186 million on the table. The government decided not to penalize the citizens of Quebec because there was no agreement. We decided, within our own jurisdiction, to cut income tax up to $85 with that money for Quebec residents who pay taxes. We chose 1977 over 1978 because we wanted that money to be in the Quebec economy right away. If we had waited, the money would not have been in the Quebec economy until next spring. If Mr. Parizeau has to raise some money because he made a miscalculation in his budget, he can do it tomorrow. He could have done it yesterday. He can do whatever he wants, in his jurisdiction.
If he needs more money because he could not come to terms with the federal government, that is up to him. He can raise sales taxes, he can raise income taxes, he can raise corporation taxes, he can invent a new tax within his own jurisdiction. We decided that $186 million was available, but he did not take it up in the national program so we are sending back to Quebec taxpayers amounts up to $85. We want it to be done as quickly as possible.
We do not know what kind of system Mr. Parizeau will choose in order to raise this money or other moneys. Some 200,000 people in Quebec will not receive the $85. Because we had already given a tax exemption of $100 in January and February, we chose 1977, as well as the fact that the money will come into the economy right away. The problem did not arise in the other provinces, because there was a national agreement with them. We reduced our income tax and they increased theirs and used the money to cut the sales tax in the way we wanted. The money is flowing into provincial coffers because of the agreement between the other provinces and the federal government. The money will flow into the provincial economies from April 10 until October 10.

Mr. Chairman, in answer to an earlier question, I believe the minister stated that one of the reasons he did not want to make a payment to the other provinces who preferred to go the deduction route was that he did not want to pass through the expenditure column at the federal level whatever the amount would have been, say $800 million. I think he pointed to the members on this side of the House as those who would have complained if he had increased his spending. Would the minister state if 1 am correct in understanding that as one of the reasons for his favouring the deduction route for the other provinces, as opposed to some type of expenditure route?

Mr. Chairman, what we have done is simple. We decided the night of the budget that we would reduce personal income tax where there Was an agreement for cutting sales tax. Legally, the only thing we have done is reduce personal income tax by $100 in provinces except Quebec and Alberta, for different reasons. We asked the provinces, in
June 13, 1978

return, to raise income tax and, with the proceeds, reduce sales tax.
The federal government will verify the books at the end of the year. If we have cut our tax too much in relation to the amount the provinces need, they are to return some money to us. On the other hand, if we have not cut income tax enough and the provinces spend more in reducing sales tax, the federal government will compensate for the difference. What we have done is to reduce the income tax of federal taxpayers in all the provinces except Quebec and Alberta.

Mr. Chairman, the minister will save a lot of time this evening if he will try to answer the questions. Specifically, did I understand him correctly when he explained why he chose to go the reduction route which he has just described with the other provinces? Mr. Chairman, I said this afternoon, and I repeat it: yes. One reason was that we were to reduce our income tax, thus making room for the provinces who agreed to raise their own income tax and with their profits they would cut their sales tax. We operated in that way because it was the best way to reduce our taxes-in other words, our take from taxpayers federally-and make sure that the money was directed in the best way to stimulate the economy.

Why has he adopted a concept of paying S85 per person to residents of Quebec which will increase spending in some fiscal year?

Mr. Chairman, the $85 for taxpayers of Quebec is a reduction in taxes. We will be reducing the taxes of those taxpayers by $85. It will not be seen as an expenditure. It is a reduction of taxes on the taxes we received from those taxpayers in 1977. It is not an expenditure.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose we should all study to see how the minister twists an $85 payment going back to the residents of Quebec into something that he said is not a federal expenditure. I am willing to acknowledge that he is pigeon-holing it; he is neatly saying that in his mind the $85 is a refund on 1977 tax payable. But 1 suggest that surely it has to go through an account somewhere and would normally show as an expenditure, perhaps with respect to refunds in a previous year, in this case 1978.

Mr. Chairman, it is a reduction of the tax paid by taxpayers in 1977. It is not an expenditure; it is a reduction of the tax liability of Quebec taxpayers for 1977. That is not a payment and it will not be written in the books as an expenditure of the government. It will be a reduction of the revenue, which is another way of saying a reduction in taxes.

Mr. Chairman, let us put it this way. Will the Quebec moneys, whether they are an expenditure, a refund, a reduction or however the minister would like to term it, be reflected in the 1978 fiscal year for the government?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

As I am speaking, the federal government is collecting $100 less for every taxpayer in the other provinces, except Quebec and Alberta, and at the same time, Ontario and Manitoba taxpayers are paying their respective provincial governments $100 more, and with their profits, these provinces are reducing their taxes. As we are collecting their taxes on their behalf, we are of course making payments to them on a six month basis beginning in April.

Mr. Chairman, I will take another run at it. The minister has identified the fact that the Quebec payment, be it a refund, an expenditure or whatever, will fall into the federal government's fiscal 1978 figures; in other words, the March 31, 1978, fiscal year end. My second question was, where will the other amount fall: will it fall into fiscal 1979?

In both cases, Mr. Chairman, the payments will be made during the taxpayers' year, because the taxpayers' year is not the same as the government's fiscal year. The taxpayers' year is 1978. The government's fiscal year is from April 1, 1978 to March 31, 1979. In both cases, payments will be made on the basis of the 1978-79 income year; as to the federal government's revenues, that is the 1978-79 fiscal year.

Surely the minister cannot have it both ways: it is something that will be reflected in fiscal 1978-which I presume it is, if it is a refund

for 1977 taxes-or, in fact, it is not as he has been representing it to be, and that is a refund for 1977. Would the minister clarify that? I am talking about two different types of situations. As far as the fiscal books are concerned, will the Quebec payments be relfected in fiscal 1978 and, second, will the payments with respect to the other provinces be reflected in fiscal 1979?

Mr. Chairman, the reductions will fall into the federal government's fiscal year 1978-79. As we have been contemplating certain amendments to clause 30, will the minister indicate whether he would entertain an amendment which would have the effect of simply putting the Quebec situation on a basis comparable to that of other provinces, rather than having this $85 going out in a cheque in relation to 1977? Mr. Chairman, I cannot accept that proposal because it would not be acceptable to the Quebec government. In his letter, Mr. Parizeau demanded in addition the payment of interest, something which was not provided in all payments made to the other provinces and since that aspect is not acceptable this is why we are not prepared to entertain any amendment to clause 30(a) or 30(b).

Mr. Chairman, will the minister clarify whether it is simply the payment of interest that is the reason he does not want to go along with that proposal, or are there other reasons why he does not want to accept the proposal I have made?

On several occasions, I explained to the House all the reasons why the government has suggested when it introduced Bill C-56 an immediate refund of $85 to Quebec taxpayers. We wanted that incentive to be injected immediately in the Quebec economy. We also wanted to cover 200,000 taxpayers who would not be included if we take the 1978 taxpayers' roll because having already received a $100 reduction, then they would not qualify for the $85 refund. The third reason is that if I agreed to the proposal of the hon. member for York-Simcoe, the money would be injected into the Quebec economy only in the spring of 1979 and in the case of taxpayers filing their income tax return late, either in March or April, before the tax returns could be analysed and finalized

many among them would receive their refund only in June and even perhaps in July 1979.

Across Canada?

I suggest to the minister that the payment of $186 million to Quebec is quite different from that being given to the province of Ontario or the province of Manitoba. In order for them to get the abatement through income tax, the room left in the $100, they must have a sales tax cut. The province of Quebec is not under the obligation to have a sales tax cut, or has not assumed it is going to have a sales tax cut. Therefore, there is a fundamental difference between the two payments. I would regard the $186 million injected into the Quebec economy as a payment to individuals. Before it can be earned in the other provinces or abated by the federal government, there must be a sales tax cut. That must reflect in the actual purchasing of consumer goods, which will stimulate business, which is what the minister indicated in the first place.

That is exactly the point I have been trying to make for two months. That is because Quebec has not come into the national scheme. They left on the table $186 million, because they qualified for $40 million of the $226 million which we had planned as our contribution to an across-the-board cut of two points for six months.
As they did not agree to the national scheme, they left $186 million on the table. Rather than penalize Quebec's citizens, we decided to cut the income tax for an equivalent amount to the benefit of taxpayers in that province. We did not sign an agreement with Quebec because Quebec did not want to sign the same agreement as the others. It was always envisaged by my ministry that if we could not get everyone to agree, there would be another income tax cut; but we preferred our policy of cutting sales taxes. We decided we would deal with the provinces in which there was a sales tax, and since there was $186 million left we further decided to cut income tax to the taxpayers in Quebec by that amount.

I understand that direct tax remissions made to citizens tend to be put into savings, whereas in order to save under sales tax cuts, citizens have to buy something. Has the minister any estimate of the effects of the economic stimulus brought about by the injection of $186 million into the economy as a cash payment, as opposed to the effect of cuts in sales tax of a similar amount?

We have not made that calculation. But I have always said I would much have preferred Quebec to join the national scheme. As the province has not done so, we have decided to cut the income tax of federal taxpayers in Quebec by $85. We recognize it would have been better for the national economy had Quebec joined in the sales tax cut agreement.

This is a type of non-tariff barrier by selective cuts, and at least it is a change. Presumably, Quebec looked over the range of goods it manufactured and tended to favour its own economy. In the rest of the country, Quebec would have the benefit, whatever it might be, of the lower sales tax, and in essence the provincial treasury is protected since it has lost only $20 million as far as the 3 per cent is concerned. It seems to me the effect has been a non-tariff barrier to some extent inasmuch as the Quebec sales tax has remained the same as they affect industries which are not prominent in that province.

The intention of the Parti Quebecois is clear. They have issued communications indicating they took the course they did in a protectionist frame of mind to aid the Quebec economy. The other day the hon. member for Levis read a letter in this House which was really quite funny. On June 3, Mr. Parizeau wrote a letter to the shoe manufacturers of Quebec who had asked him to cut the sales tax on shoes. He said that to cut the taxes from 8 per cent to zero would be no good at all; that such a policy would make no sense. That was his view in January. But he did a complete about turn in April so as to undermine the national scheme. They were doing it in the way in which the hon. member suggests, in a protectionist spirit for the sake of their own economy.
In the case of shoes, according to the letter written by Mr. Parizeau to the shoe manufacturers, more than 60 per cent of the shoes sold in Quebec do not come from Quebec. In fact, more come from Ontario than from Quebec. But the avowed intention of the government was to protect its own economy and to try to break the so-called national common market. We have not yet made a study to determine whether their scheme is better than ours. If all the provinces were to go ahead on a selective tax basis, Ontario would probably prefer to cut sales tax on automobiles, British Columbia would go for building materials, and the maritimes, Saskatchewan and Manitoba would have chosen products appropriate to them.
The argument which I used in the west was this: even though you do not have a manufacturing base of great strength, half of the cost in the retail economy is not the cost of production but the cost of services-transportation, publicity, storage, and so on. These factors make up half the cost of all goods bought from a store. That is how I persuaded them to

June 13, 1978
Income Tax Act
join the scheme. It was designed to stimulate the retail business in the local economies. But the Quebec government has claimed over and over again that Mr. Parizeau was out to be a protectionist and did not give a damn about the Canadian market.

I understand from some figures given out at the conference held in Montreal that Quebec benefits more than any other province from the Canadian market in commodities because it produces goods which, by and large, have greater sales in the rest of Canada than do the goods of most of the other regions.

If we look at the general aspect of the Canadian economy, Quebec is not the province which benefits most from the domestic market. Ontario, which has a much larger share of the manufacturing sector, benefits more than Quebec. This is one of the criticisms directed at me during the preparation of my program-that I was helping Ontario more than Quebec. It could be true that this program is helping Ontario more than Quebec, but I would point out it is helping Quebec more than any of the other eight provinces. Some clothing is manufactured in Manitoba, but the part of it which goes into the local economy is less than in Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that this piece of legislation has created provinces with special status. It seems obvious that the minister was anxious to bring down a budget at this time because he was posturing in preparation for a July election. Earlier today the hon. gentleman told the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that he would welcome input from a committee of this House, and that he was a great believer in the principle of participatory democracy. It is hard to believe this is the same minister who has brought in closure on two occasions in connection with the legislation before us. That is a fine way to support participatory democracy.

1 wish to raise a point of order, Mr. Chairman. We have so far spent 19 days in debate on this measure. We are on clause 30, and at second reading this legislation was filibustered for 11 or 12 days. We could have reached clause 30 a long time ago. There is no precedent for such a long debate on a tax bill.
Hon. members have been rambling without dealing with the clauses. We spent two days on clause 1. There was general debate, and the hon. member is still making general comments. We had an occasion this afternoon to talk about time allocation. Hon. members opposite did not want to speak at that time; they wanted to discuss clause 30. The hon. member should ask questions and I would be happy to reply. He had 19 days in which to speak, but was not seen in the House on those days.

Mr. Chairman, my comments are related to clause 30. It is interesting, the degree to which the minister has been participating in this debate ever since he brought in

closure. This afternoon, when he was speaking, he went on for approximately 15 minutes on one answer which could have been given in two minutes. If the minister is serious in criticizing me for going on, he should take a little advice himself.
Ask a question.

As has been said on many occasions in this House, Alberta has no sales tax and that is why Alberta originally agreed to the proposal put forward by the minister. However, when Albertans became aware that the minister was going to give an $85 rebate to Quebeckers for the 1977 taxation year, they became concerned. It is obvious that some individuals will participate twice under this proposal. If a Quebec resident moved to Ontario but filed his 1977 tax form in Quebec, would he be eligible for the $85 rebate, while at the same time being able to take advantage of the sales tax reductions in Ontario?

Mr. Chairman, any citizen who moves from one province to another finds himself in a different situation. If a citizen of Ontario moves to Quebec, or the reverse takes place, he will qualify because the list for 1977 is used. If somebody moves to Newfoundland, he moves to an 11 per cent sales tax rate. If he moves from Alberta, he leaves a province where there is no sales tax. It is a person's own choice. We will take the list of 1977 taxpayers. The same thing would happen if we used the 1978 list, because there is movement of people during the year.

It is obvious that an individual who moves out of Quebec will receive the $85 rebate. In addition, he will have the advantage of living in a province where sales tax is reduced, so in essence there will be a double benefit. Earlier this afternoon we heard from the minister about the great concessions being offered to Alberta with regard to the heavy oil industry. It should be pointed out to the minister that these concessions are not simply for Albertans; they are for all Canadians. When we review what Albertans have contributed to confederation through our oil and natural gas industries, we find that because our prices are below the world price, Alberta has saved Canadians about $10 billion. I think that is a significant contribution to confederation on the part of Albertans.
It becomes more and more obvious that this government has no concern whatsoever for the province of Alberta. This has even been stated by this government's own Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce: he has stated that the government has no feeling for Alberta whatsoever. Just to substantiate my point, I would like to read a couple of lines from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. In a Canadian Press story headed "Horner says Post "Lonely", we find the following:
Jack Horner says he has had a lonely first year as federal Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
Horner told a nominating convention recently he is frustrated because there is no one else in the cabinet "who really deeply cares about the province of Alberta."

Order.
June 13, 1978
Do you want him to table it?

The truth seems to hurt my hon. friends. It can be documented that over and over again Alberta has been shortchanged under numerous government programs. We can read about the contract awards of the Department of Supply and Services. The former minister of national defence, the hon. member for Winnipeg South, has stated that he hopes to see equitable spending in all government departments. This matter has been pursued by numerous hon. members on this side of the House. Various government programs are not equitable as far as Alberta is concerned.
Clause 30, Mr. Chairman.
With regard to clause 30, Mr. Chairman-
Hear, hear!

-hon. members opposite feel that theirs is the only party to keep this country together. The leader of my party has spoken about this. The proposals in clause 30 are a fine example of the disunity the Liberal party is creating within Canada. The Minister of Finance claims that we, as federal Conservatives, are in bed with the Quebec separatists simply because we support the position which has been taken unanimously in the Quebec National Assembly. We have the Minister of Transport who says we are spreading anti-Quebec lies and hatred across the west.
I would like to share with the House what a journalist in the Montreal Star has said about this. He is curious as to how we can be in bed with one group while at the same time hating them. It is ironic that one minister says we hate them, and another says we are in bed with them. However, that is the kind of trickery we see far too often on the part of hon. members opposite. That concludes my remarks on clause 30.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to follow up my comments on second reading and ask whether the minister received any formal objections from the government of Alberta or a minister of the government of Alberta when the sales tax rebate for Quebec was modified to become an income tax rebate in the amount of $186 million.

Mr. Chairman, I spoke to Mr. Leitch about this. I informed him of my plans. I do not recall exactly what he said. He did not write me a letter or communicate any formal protest. We discussed the matter. Everyone at that time was very sorry that the Quebec government did not agree to the national scheme. Everyone understood that I was doing my best to solve a difficult problem. Hon. members can understand the frustration we all felt. Of course, I took the brunt of it. Mr. McKeough of Ontario has made two speeches about this. The others kept rather silent about it, but they understood that they were to come out on the day of the budget with a "yes" or "no". Quebec did not respect that commitment, and that put everyone in a difficult position.
I explained what I was trying to do, that I was trying to solve the problem as best I could, and before I tabled this bill I
Income Tax Act
informed the provincial ministers of my intentions. I cannot say that all provincial ministers rejoiced. They were quite sorry and their reaction was, "Jean, do your best". They did not raise any formal protest, but I must recognize that they were not happy.

I am sure the minister is correct when he says he was encouraged to do his best after the difficult fiasco he got himself into. I ask him whether there were objections to the proposals contained in clause 30 long before the Quebec government made known its objections to the sales tax rebate. I am referring to the meeting of the four western premiers: they met shortly after the budget was announced in this House on April 10. The western premiers took very strong exception on two counts, not one, of intrusion into provincial jurisdiction.

It is not what they said, Mr. Chairman. I would like to correct the hon. member. He should read the letter of the Prime Minister in reply to Mr. Blakeney who wrote on behalf of the western premiers. They said they agreed with the substance of the proposition but they were not satisfied with the extent of consultation. I have explained to the House many times that when they agreed with the substance and complained about the form, they were not talking about invasion of their jurisdiction.
With regard to the extent of consultations, I have explained to the House all the limitations 1 have in terms of consultations. I went to all the provinces to meet their ministers of finance. I was faced with the possibility of an eventual leak, which actually occurred in a column by Dalton Camp in the Toronto Star the night before the budget. Everyone knows that I am not in daily communication with Dalton Camp. I never talked to him in my life. I do not know where the leak came from, but he had the full story.
They agreed with the substance of the proposal but complained about the extent of consultation. It is the kind of statement that is so easy to make. We have spent 20 days on this bill and only today did we start to move on to other clauses; yet people still rise and say that not enough time was given. We have to make a decision once in a while if we want the House to operate. When I was in England, 1 felt sad that we do not operate our House of Commons in the same way as the British. They would never spend 20 days on a bill.

Mr. Chairman. I should like to point out to the minister that England is a unitary state, not a federal state, and therein lies the difference when you talk about consultation. I have another question for the minister. There is a distinct difference of interpretation here. I believe he has agreed with me that the western premiers were not pleased with the consultative approach. I do not think many arguments have come forward to the minister, from any quarter, that the reduction of the direct retail sales tax is the quickest way to stimulate retail buying. You have no argument from me on that score.

June 13, 1978
Income Tax Act
The point 1 am trying to make-1 think the minister has to concede it - is that whether we say consultations were sufficient, or not, is at this point not something with which I will agree. But the point that must be made is that the western premiers were saying that the consultations had not gone far enough in that there was an encroachment into provincial jurisdiction. That point must be made. The minister mentioned earlier that there will be federal reinbursement to these provinces for lost revenue, for the 2 per cent reduction in sales tax over a six-month period. To what extent will this increase the deficit in current accounts?

We have operated through an income tax cut across the board, and the calculation was that the federal share of this program would be $1.1 billion. The federal cost was about $680 million-I speak from memory-and half of it would come from a reduction in our own expenditures of, say, $340 million: the other $340 million was to be added to the deficit, or the cash requirements. So before the budget was brought down, the cash requirements were about $11.1 billion and I said that the cash requirement would be about $11.5 billion, an increase of some $350 million. So the total package was $1.1 billion and the cost in terms of our deficit would be about $350 million.

I take it from the minister's comments, to confirm what he said earlier, that the extra draw on the federal treasury will bring the projected deficit to $11.5 billion. The minister has mentioned that approximately $340 million or $350 million will be saved in the sense that expenditures will be cut back in that order. Can he indicate, in broad terms, where those savings will take place?

Mr. Chairman, the President of the Treasury Board is working on the program. In the letter which was circulated, the Prime Minister gave orders to the various departments to come up with plans for a reduction in expenditures. We are in the process of doing that internally. When the program is completed, the announcement will be made.

Will the reduction of approximately $340 million or $350 million be from the expenditures that were deemed to be passed on May 31? I know that some committees kept on meeting after that date. Were those the expenditures from which savings are to take place?
We are having to reduce expenditures in the fiscal year 1978-79.

I should like to ask the minister the following question: There has been a fair amount of discussion of the fact that the provinces had to go along with the plan, and 1 am not saying whether the plan was good, bad or indifferent. In the past we had what is known as a 50-cent dollar; in other words, the federal government makes cost-sharing arrangements under which the provinces, especially those with lower per capita incomes, simply must take part in the program because of the argument that it is a 50 per cent cost rather than a 100 per cent cost to the provincial treasury.

In this case, one could argue that the federal government was advancing a 66%-cent dollar to the provinces. Has the minister had any consultation with the provinces as to what effect the reimposition of the sales tax will have on Canada's economic situation as we go into the winter months of 197879? It is hypothetical in one sense, and in another it is not; but I wonder what will happen to the Canadian economy when the provinces reimpose the sales tax at its level prior to the April 10 budget.

We have looked into that. We felt that reintroduction of the sales tax, if the provinces decide to reintroduce it in mid-October, will come at the time of an increase in sales because of the pre-Christmas period. We have looked at the experience of Ontario which tried that two years ago; that was what started the wheels rolling. We have reason to believe there must be a difference in the economy, sometimes, between what is an investment and what is a non-investment, if production is reflected in the increase from the 83-cent dollar to the 89-cent dollar. This is the kind of push that can get the wheels rolling in the right direction; everyone has recognized that. Of course, when the time comes in the fall when the sales tax is reintroduced by the provinces who need the money, they will not be as completely happy with it as they were to join this program.
I would like to say to the hon. member, who comes from Manitoba, that sales in that province since the April 10 budget have increased substantially. I met someone from Winnipeg the other day, when I was in Toronto to make a speech, who told me that he is a good friend of the minister of finance in Manitoba, Mr. Craik, who said that sales tax revenues are increasing very satisfactorily. As I was saying this afternoon, if increases in sales are in the order of 15 per cent in that period, the province will have recaptured all the money it has invested in the program. This is not so in my case because I am not collecting the sales tax alone; I will lose the revenue completely.

Mr. Chairman, it has been my theory all along that excessive taxation acts as a damper rather than a generator of revenue. Very often the government takes revenue out of private hands, thus reducing spending power. Obviously, the provinces will speak on their own behalf at the end of the six-month or nine-month period. The provinces had very little choice because two-thirds of the sales tax savings was to be advanced by the federal government.
Have projections been done, based on the early part of 1979? Generally, retail sales rise in the last quarter as a result of Christmas sales. Traditionally there is a dramatic slump in the first quarter of the year. Are we selling 1979 potential sales in 1978? This could have an adverse effect on the high unemployment and high cost months of the first quarter of 1979.

It is not shifting the time of buying. Perhaps that will be the effect in some cases, but that is not the
June 13, 1978

intention. Perhaps a person who wants to buy a television, an automobile, or something like that, will do so right away. It is intended to be a boost to the economy. At the present time, there is a difficulty because Canadians are not spending some of their savings. For the third year in a row we have been faced with record levels of savings-11.5 per cent. 1 am not saying that people should not save, but perhaps they should save a little less in order to stimulate the economy.
As the hon. member indicated earlier, the fastest way to get the ball rolling is to stimulate the economy through a reduction in retail sales tax. This is the first time it has been attempted and it is unfortunate that Quebec did not agree. I should like to thank all ministers of finance, except the Quebec minister, for collaborating in this great scheme. Of course, the Quebec minister of finance is attempting to prove that confederation is not working, but I am sure that view is not shared by the hon. member.

At the present time there is an income tax rebate in the order of $85 per federal income taxpayer in the province of Quebec, for a total of approximately $186 million. The March, 1977, budget did not stimulate the economy as hoped; therefore, the route employing a reduction in sales tax was taken by the minister. In view of the fact that Canadian savings are at an all-time high, what portion of that $186 million which will be reimbursed to Quebec federal income tax payers will be savings?

Mr. Chairman, it is impossible to make such a calculation. We recognize that some people will save their rebates. We hope they will not, but it is impossible to arrive at an exact figure. In January and February there was an income tax cut of $100 because of the mini-budget of October 20, 1977. We realize that some of that money went into savings but we cannot measure precisely the amount; we could only make a guess.

The minister's tax cuts took place in January and February, and now taxpayers of the province of Quebec will benefit by another rebate. To what extent will the economy of Quebec be stimulated by the $186 million, as opposed to the $40 million which resulted from direct sales tax cuts on selective items?

As I said earlier, I would have preferred it if Quebec had joined the national scheme; there is no doubt about that. But that province did not want to participate in the same manner as the other provinces. As money was left over, we decided to reduce income taxes. That was a second best proposal. Perhaps Quebec feels its selective tax cuts were a better approach. It would have been nice if Quebec had mentioned its proposition during our three weeks of consultation. In that event, perhaps I would have joined with Quebec in believing that they had a good scheme. It was raised as a possibility 48 hours after I had given my word, on behalf of the federal government, to the other eight provincial minister of finance. Thus, we decided to take the second best route by giving a tax rebate.
Income Tax Act

I should like to return to the situation in Alberta which has been raised by other hon. members. If my understanding of per capita income is correct, Albertans enjoy the second highest in Canada, Ontario being the highest. If a person in Alberta makes "X" number of dollars and has the same family responsibilities as a person in any of the other provinces earning the same amount, what rationale is there for not providing a rebate to an Albertan? He will not receive any income tax or sales tax rebate. Of course, he could not receive a sales tax rebate because he was not required to pay one. But when the rebate was changed to an income tax rebate, a federal taxpayer in Quebec would receive two advantages. First, he would receive the income tax rebate because of his residency in Quebec. Then, if he moved to a province which received the benefit of sales tax reduction, he would receive another advantage.
How can the minister rationalize the statements of the Prime Minister indicating that that is not a special deal, particularly when one considers that residents of Alberta are left out in the cold without either a sales tax or income tax rebate?

That answer was given to the committee a couple of minutes ago. We were faced with a situation similar to one in which two individuals made $10,000 each. One paid sales tax and the other did not. We decided to benefit the person who was paying sales tax. I had occasion to call Mr. Merv Leitch in Alberta to indicate that we wanted to cut the sales tax of the province. He indicated that they did not have a sales tax. Thus, my proposition was not feasible. We were interested in assisting those who were required to pay sales taxes. In order to treat everyone equally it would be necessary to have a sales tax system across Canada applied uniformly in each province. One must remember that the residents of the province of Newfoundland pay 11 per cent sales tax on everything they buy, whereas Albertans are not required to pay any. They are not in the same situation. In such a scheme nobody is in exactly the same situation.
The government paid all the costs for the maritime provinces because we felt they could not afford to participate using their own money. We made a special case with Saskatchewan and British Columbia because they had a specific problem. In the case of Alberta, they do not have a rebate because we made money available only to the provinces where there was a sales tax. However, we are very preoccupied with the economy of Alberta; for example, we have given some stimulus to the heavy oil scheme. There is no heavy oil scheme in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island or Newfoundland. There is no discrimination against any of the other provinces because heavy oil is found only in Alberta, and probably will be in north Saskatchewan one day. The government wishes to help this type of economy because it is good for the country. There are different situations for different taypayers because there is not the same level across-the-board in Canada. It varies from one province to another.

June 13, 1978
Income Tax Act

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, 1 listened with care to what the minister said, and I wanted to intervene between speakers rather than interrupt an hon. member. In the course of answering the hon. member for Pembina with respect to the time spent on this bill, the minister said there had been 20 days. The minister now indicates he was wrong in that respect. He was covering the budget period as well as this bill. The minister knows full well that the budget time is allotted under the Standing Orders. I do not want there to be any misrepresentation of the factual situation with respect to the time on this bill, however inadvertent it might be. I am sure, too, that the minister would not want to mislead the House in that way.

Mr. Chairman, I will be extremely precise: six days on the budget debate, 14 days on this bill. This amounts to about two months of the work of the government because the rest of the time is taken, more or less, by opposition days in this House. We have not yet completed debate because there are two more days to go, and we have third reading. I wish, as the hon. member said earlier, we could import some of the good, British tradition- and for a French Canadian like me to want to import British tradition is something-and have the power to say that the debate will last three or four days. The British do not spend 20 or 30 days on a tax bill. It is my hope that we will import some of the British common sense into this House.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether that is government policy or not, but it is very interesting. The government seems to be moving in this way and I am delighted to see my friend attracted to British traditions to such a great degree. I know that it has not escaped him, however, that during the course of this bill we have been in the unprecedented position, with respect to a tax bill, to have closure within two stages of the bill within days of one another, or time allocation, to be more precise: but a rose by any other name is still a rose.
I want to make it clear to the minister that he can hold his view with respect to time, as I can mine, but there is only one view with respect to the facts. I am sure it was through inadvertence that the minister was talking in terms of a 20-day debate on this bill. He has now cleared that up and I am grateful to him.
[ Translation]

Mr. Chairman since the Quebec government decided not to accept the finance minister's proposal contained in the budget, I would like to know why the minister took exception to Mr. Parizeau's proposal of giving the approximately $200 million difference from the sales tax to the Quebec government? He was to give that money to the Quebec government rather than refunding $85 to some taxpayers.

That is very simple, Mr. Chairman. If the hon. member followed the debate, and being a conscientious member, I am sure he did, he will remember that on budget

night we reduced the income tax of taxpayers in the eight provinces party to the program. Quebec did not qualify for the program, except for an equivalent of $40 million which I am ready to pay. It left $186 million on the table. So we reduced the income tax in the other provinces. We are reducing the income tax of Quebec residents. It is as simple as that. We are rebating the federal income tax paid by the taxpayers, since we are not collecting the Quebec government's taxes because there was no collection agreement. If Mr. Parizeau has to increase his taxes tomorrow, the day after, next month or next year, that is his business. Since the time of Maurice Duplessis, it has been important for Quebec to collect its own taxes. Being of the Mauricie region, I am sure that Maurice must have turned in his grave when he saw Mr. Parizeau asking me to collect taxes for him, because that is the greatest sin against autonomy. Duplessis would never have done that. Barrette would never have done that. Sauve would never have done that. Lesage would never have done that. Johnson would never have done that. Bertrand would never have done that, and Bourassa would never have done that.
Neither would I!
Neither would he. But Mr. Parizeau did. The virginity of Quebeckers was worth $185 million. What do you want me to do about it?
Quite so, but you say that you would hand over an amount of $40 million to the province of Quebec in an envelope-
Yes.
-and they turned it down?
Yes.
Then they agreed and you are going to hand the money over to them in an envelope?

We are going to send approximately $40 million in equal payments for April, May, June, July, August and September. For the rest, we are going to grant a tax cut to all taxpayers. Why have we decided on this method? Because there is no tax collection agreement with the province of Quebec. In the other provinces, the operation was painless. On budget night, I reduced the federal tax by $100. The finance ministers in Ontario or New Brunswick increased their respective taxes by $100. And with the profits they made, they will reduce their sales tax by 3 per cent on all goods for the next six months. However, Quebec refused to go along with this scheme. Quebec did what it wanted to do. When some say that I infringed upon provincial jurisdictions, that is not true. Not at all! In proof of this, Mr. Parizeau did what he wanted, exactly what he wanted, I did not stop him. It was in his jurisdiction. And as for me, I do what I want, that is I cut the taxes of Quebec taxpayers by $85 as soon as possible.
June 13, 1978

Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out to the minister that I knew the answers to the questions I just asked, but I ask them as the man in the street would ask them now because he believes all the press reports and he says: the federal government has interfered with the provincial government's business, and so forth, he says that Mr. Parizeau is the saviour of New France. I want to know why and where?

That is exactly the problem, because everybody got excited as though it were a constitutional problem. Here is what I did: on the very first day I said that the sales tax came under provincial jurisdiction because I phoned the provincial finance ministers I told them: "Gentlemen, you have a so-called sales tax; could I help you to reduce it? I will pay you 2 per cent during six months. If you cut it by 3 per cent for six months, you will pay the difference". Eight ministers of finance said: "Yes, Mr. Chretien, we agree". The discussions went on for three weeks. During those three weeks, the Quebec finance minister, Mr. Parizeau, remained silent. When the agreement was concluded with the other finance ministers, he said 48 hours later: "I do not want that, I want something else. He had missed the boat.
The train!

It is quite simple. I had given my word to the other finance ministers. It is like the train, but I will not repeat the saying about watching the train go by, but it is as simple as that. It is just as if the hon. member for Richmond were going with ten others. There is a car or a small bus going to Montreal. After the bus has left, someone aboard says: No, I want to go to Quebec city." The others tell him: "Listen, this bus is going to Montreal. We cannot go to Montreal and to Quebec city at the same time." So the one who wants to go to Quebec city has to walk because the bus only goes to Montreal. It is as simple as that. If Mr. Parizeau had been willing to discuss, it would have been all so simple. But I said it before and I say it again: the Quebec government is bent on proving that everything we are doing now is wrong. Even before the paper on the renewal of the Canadian Federation was published, even before he got a copy. Mr. Levesque said: "It is profoundly insignificant". He had not even read it yet.
That is what we want to know.

As I said, they are bent on proving that federalism cannot work. No wonder! But when I simply proposed to help them cut their sales tax, they all took refuge behind the constitution. There is no constitutional problem at all in all this, there has never been and there will never be. The sales tax comes under provincial jurisdiction, I admitted it and said: "I will help you." It is as if 1 told the hon. member it is his business if he wants to go home. But if I offer to pay two-thirds of his trip, he can tell me to go to hell. Only, if he
Income Tax Act
wants to pocket the money, I shall be very happy to give it to him.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to tell the Minister of Finance that if he had given the very simple explanation he has just given me also to the journalists, there are still some left who are honest, things would not have been as complicated as they have been with the province of Quebec in the last three months.

Mr. Chairman, I agree wholeheartedly. I tried for all I am worth to give that explanation. I was given a chance to explain myself only last week, seven weeks after, when the French network of the CBC invited to me to appear on the program Telescopie for 25 minutes. All that network did until then was to run around the halls and find people who were against the idea.
Like the hon. member for Joliette.

They avoided the people who were for it. It is as clear as that. It is painful, but that is democracy. I am not complaining too much about it, Mr. Chairman, because it must be remembered that one has to be in good health to put up with a system like that. Let me explain: I am glad to see the hon. member understands and is asking questions so people will understand. I am not personally worried about the people from that point of view. They have a lot more judgment than they are often given credit for and the best proof of that is that in spite of the great controversy over the sales tax our rating increased according to the Gallup poll.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister of Finance a question about the proposal he allegedly made to all provincial ministers of finance to reduce the sales tax by 3 per cent where his contribution would be 2 per cent on all products in all Canadian industries and all retail sales outlets across Canada, in face of the refusal of Mr. Parizeau who preferred a selective sales tax.
Could the minister say whether from the point of view of the collection of a selective sales tax such a collection could pose problems with respect to forecasts or lower revenues because according to what we hear, and I heard it said as recently as this past weekend, some retailers because certain products do not qualify for the sales tax cut in Quebec would want to use other products and thus the province would be deprived of revenues because this would mean a reduced tax base for the province of Quebec and then there could be a danger if the sales tax were less than anticipated that Mr. Parizeau would be tempted to increase his taxes next year and perhaps call it "Chretien's" tax. Could the minister say whether this would make sense, that the selective sales tax cut could result in reduced revenues and an increase in taxes next year in Mr. Parizeau's budget?

June 13, 1978
Income Tax Act

Of course, the question is whether the implementation of a selective tax cut from 8 per cent down to nothing will result in an administrative problem to the Quebec revenue department. I do not know. Let me say the temptation is great, and I give you an example, and I say it is very complicated-if you buy furniture there is no sales tax but if you buy a television set there is a sales tax. They say that sometimes people might put down "chair" instead of "television" on a bill. I do not know about this. It is up to the Quebec revenue officials to see to it that the law is obeyed. However, there is a lot of confusion because not all textile products have been exempted: You must pay 8 per cent on drapes, carpets, sheets, pillow cases, but there is no tax on other items such as suits. I have enough problems of my own without solving theirs and deciding how they will collect their taxes.
I do know one thing. When time comes to determine the consequences of all these decisions, it will be very complicated because according to our agreement with the other provinces, we shall have to check how much this has cost them. If a province which had a sales tax of 7 per cent reduces it to 4 per cent, it is very easy to know how much this costs because we shall simply transpose the whole amount of the 4 per cent tax at 7 per cent and this will give us the exact cost. It is a simple mathematical operation. It is easy to figure out. But when you talk about going from 8 per cent down to nothing, you have no data on the amount sold because you have no invoice, no account to the government, no means of control. I am not saying that it was done intentionally, I am simply saying that we have no means of control. This is where the particular problem raised by the Ontario finance minister Mr. McKeough, and his deputy minister, arises namely that according to their own extrapolation they cannot see how a selective tax cut by the Quebec government could cost Quebec $320 or $340 million. They took their own figures and made extrapolations to come to the conclusion that it would cost $250 million. I am caught between both, and as no agreement has been reached with the government of Quebec, I cannot make a judgment, I can only reduce my income tax. The financial critics of the opposition in Quebec will have to see if the Ontario government is right on that. I do not wish to interfere in the administration of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, has the minister recognized in his statement that the selective tax cuts proposed by Mr. Parizeau could mean a reduction of his revenues, next year and an increase in his next budget?

I have no comments to make as the hon. member might come to the conclusion that there are some abuses. I do not know. I do not intend to look for them, but Revenue Canada will check the amount of $40 million at the end of the year. I have no judgment to make. Since the hon. member is asking me questions about the financial situation of the government of Quebec I should point out that I am not the financial critic of the opposition in Quebec, but if I were I
would have fun. In the circumstances I must make my own fun here in Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, it was fairly obvious that the government -intended to have an election during the period this sales tax reduction was in effect. Now that we are not going to have the election, I wonder if it is the government's intention to continue the program until October 15 or 16 when it will start to expire.

Mr. Chairman, we have no such plan at this time. I know the maritime ministers of finance have made some public comments about that. I expect to have a discussion on the effect of the sales tax cut when I meet the ministers of finance on July 7 and 8.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that this program is discriminatory toward the province of Alberta, may I ask if any consideration was given to that province as its minimum wage is about 90 cents an hour less than it was in the province of Quebec when this matter was discussed?
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member please repeat his question? I am sorry, but I missed it.

Mr. Chairman, was any consideration given to the fact that the minimum wage for the province of Alberta is about 90 cents an hour less than it is in the province of Quebec, when the minister had discussions with regard to putting this program in place?

It was not under consideration. I had occasion to tell the minister of finance of Quebec at one time that having the highest minimum wage in the world was not conducive to having a very good economic situation in Quebec because having that kind of minimum wage tends to push up all the costs. This was not relative to sales tax at all; it was in another context that I raised that point.
Mr. Chairman, could the minister tell us the effect this payment to the provinces will have on equalization payments?

The effect on the equalization payments was one of the problems discussed during the three weeks that we debated with the provinces. We have devised a formula, that is written in the act, by which the equalization payments are isolated from this temporary scheme. This means that the scheme will have no effect on the equalization payments. Some of the maritime provinces were afraid they would lose on equalization payments if we did not to make provision for that. That is another example of the consultations that I had during the three weeks before the budget.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to make some remarks at the time of consideration of clause 1, but knowing the minister was nervous about general comments on clause 1 and how he wanted to proceed as quickly as possible to clause 30, I thought he would now like to hear a few of the comments I

June 13, 1978

have saved up for this occasion. I am sure the minister has heard some of these comments before.
Many times.

I am hopeful I may be able to reiterate in a different way some of the concerns that have been expressed. Particularly, I am concerned about the apparent view of the public and the media who seem to think that this bill has only to do with the provincial sales tax issue. In fact, if one can believe what one hears via the media, it only has to do with the Quebec sales tax issue. It should be obvious to anyone who has been following the debate up to clause 30 that many other issues are covered in this legislation other than sales tax.
It is obvious from the speeches the minister has heard from this side of the House that the emphasis as far as the sales tax issue is concerned has been the unusual payment-which is all I can call it-of the cash refund, a refund of tax paid relative to the 1977 taxation year to the residents of Quebec. I compare that with the remarks of the Prime Minister who earlier in this debate referred many times to the so-called tax room that the federal government has been prepared to give on the 1978 taxation of individuals in Canada.
I am not quite sure how the two relate to one another. The Prime Minister was hard-pressed to explain and he could not understand why nobody else could follow what was happening. It is also obvious that the retail sales taxes affected by the measures of the Minister of Finance are provincial measures and do not have the raison d'etre of this House in respect of their determination. The Minister of Finance has told us all about the consultations he has had with the various ministers. He has told us in a very self-righteous manner how he had almost achieved agreement with the various ministers of finance and, as well, how the province of Quebec let him down in not finally agreeing with his proposal. Not only did the province of Quebec not agree, but the minister tells us they turned around two days after he had made the announcement on his agreement with the other provinces and said they would not agree with the federal government's proposals. I find it difficult to reconcile that with the Prime Minister's great pains to explain on a number of occasions in the Houses that the treatment of all provinces was the same.
The Prime Minister went to great lengths to explain to the Leader of the New Democratic Party that he could not understand how the Leader of the New Democratic Party and other members on this side could not understand how a refund of $85 in cash against the 1977 income tax of certain taxpayers was not the same as allowing tax room-that was his expression-in the 1978 taxation year to provinces other than Quebec. One might be forgiven if he could not understand how that is not the same. But yesterday the Minister of Finance said-and I note the parliamentary secretary is nodding agreement with what I am about to say, and I am glad he is so perceptive-that he had told the minister of finance of Quebec that if he did not go along with the national scheme, the province would not qualify for the same plan as the other provinces. I do not understand-and I hope I may be forgiv-
Income Tax Act
en-if the Prime Minister said that all provinces are being treated the same, how the Minister of Finance can tell us, the House of Commons, that the treatment he was prepared to give the province of Quebec was the same as he was prepared to give the other provinces.
The Minister of Finance says he will pay it back to the taxpayers: I think that was the expression he used-he is paying it back to the taxpayers of Quebec who have already paid the money. But he knows, and 1 note that he has been very careful not to say much about this in the current debate, that Quebec taxpayers who do not pay income tax because they are too poor will not receive any benefit from the refunds paid to the taxpayers of Quebec.
I hear my colleague-

-for Brome-Missisquoi and the hon. member for Joliette who have expressed their agreement with-

-my statement.
The minister has indicated how those in British Columbia will benefit. I recognize that the taxpayers of British Columbia will benefit because the federal government is giving tax room, in the Prime Minister's words, to the taxpayers of that province. I also recognize that there is a difference in the treatment being accorded the residents of British Columbia because everybody in the province will benefit through a reduction in sales tax. People in Quebec who are not paying the sales tax will not receive that benefit.
1 said at the outset that there are many issues included in this bill. I draw attention to the fact that some of the other issues touch on personal income tax. Some of these questions were debated as we proceeded to clause 30; some were not. Touching on personal tax, we are dealing with matters such as employee loans, deferred profit-sharing plans, registered retirement savings plans, life insurance in more than one way-I will come back to that in a moment-and the transfer of family farms. I might say another word about that in a moment. There are also measures in this bill dealing with corporation tax, such as surplus stripping and other matters dealing with life insurance companies as opposed to life insurance and the individual.
The minister likes to assure us that everything in this bill is simple, that it will all be understood by the people and that we should have no hesitation in passing his wonderful measures. I want to refer to an article in the April, 1978, CA Magazine. It makes an observation on the 3 per cent inventory allowance which 1 questioned in some detail last time the minister presented us with a bill such as this. I quote from CA Magazine:
The government therefore was introducing an annual allowance, equal to 3 per cent of the tax cost of qualifying inventory on hand at the start of the year, as a deduction in computing income from a business. That seemed simple enough,

June 13, 1978
Income Tax Act
and when the amendment was introduced and eventually passed in the fall of 1977, few people challenged the legislation in terms of whether it was workable.
Most businesses have now completed the first fiscal period for which the inventory allowance applies and the problem areas have begun to surface: basic issues such as what kinds of inventory qualify, under what circumstances and when. That these problems, and the lack of answers, did not come up earlier is undoubtedly due largely to the apparant simplicity of the provision and also to the fact that many people were focusing their attention on timing rather than substance.
I make that reference to indicate that the minister and his officials who sit waiting for something to do should be considering the real effect of that measure, and some of the measues contained in the bill before us, on the business community and individuals before so glibly assuring the House that there is no problem and these matters should be passed quite easily. To support that contention I refer to the tax letter issued on April 10, 1978, by Peat, Marwick, Mitchell and Company, an international firm of chartered accountants which makes reference to the provisions concerning insurance companies. I quote from the tax letter as follows:
An unintended result of the 1977 technical changes would have eliminated from any future deduction for certain life insurers, non-capital losses in existence as at December 31, 1977. It is proposed that such losses be restored as non-capital losses of the 1977 taxation year.
I am a chartered accountant, not a lawyer. However, I think that unintended result was dealt with by the minister in the presentation he made to the House. The point I am making is that the intentions of the minister are so unclear, when we come to clause by clause study, that it is very difficult for us to know exactly what is meant. If it is difficult for us, I am sure it is far more difficult for the average Canadian to know what is intended by the minister.
I think we will be coming to other clauses of this bill which will deal with the individual and insurance policies, in particular insurance policy loan, the difficulty parliament had, the difficulty the individual holder of a life insurance policy had, and probably what the business community and the life insurance industry had in dealing with the provisions for interest on insurance policy loans and the accounting thereof in the last budget. I thought we buried that issue the last time we had a budget debate. I again quote from the Peat, Marwick, Mitchell letter:
It is proposed that interest on policy loans made prior to April 1, 1977, would now be treated the same as interest on such loans made after March 31, 1977, i.e., deducted or added to the adjusted cost base of the policy. In addition, interest paid before 1978 on policy loans will not be included in computing the "adjusted cost base" of the policy at any time after March 31, 1978.
I hope I will be able to ask a few questions of the minister when we come to that clause. I hope the committee will agree that wording such as that, which has caused such confusion to the renowed firm of chartered accountants, Peat, Marwick, Mitchell, really has no place in the legislation we are considering. There are no fewer than two sections of the ways and means motion which deal with interest on policy loans, section 3 and section 15 which purport to deal with the adjusted cost base of a life insurance policy after March 31, 1978.
We dealt with the clauses which touch on the passing on of family farms held by corporations to the heirs. At that time 1

commented on the fact that these farm businesses were accorded different treatment from small businesses in a city constituency such as the one I represent. I also commented that I felt it unreasonable that less than six weeks after the Minister of Finance presented his budget dealing with this kind of transfer and the avoidance or deferment of capital gains tax on farm properties, the Minister of State (Small Business) introduced provisions to provide for the passing on and deferment of capital gains tax in the case of small businesses.
I might also say the minister alluded to this in answering my questions earlier-that the definition of "small business" is completely unclear in the mind of parliament. The minister has not given us the definition that we need. He said that farms are treated differently from other businesses. I want to put on record the fact that businesses which I and other city members might be familiar with are not to be considered small businesses unless they deal with such things as manufacturing, processing, wholesaling, retailing and one or two other restrictive items. The point is that no small business, regardless of its family history, concentration or anything else, will be considered eligible for the passing on of these benefits if it is involved in any kind of service business. Apparently this covers such businesses as real estate and insurance. We are not told why family businesses which happen to render services or be involved in real estate should be excluded from the benefits passed on by the Minister of State (Small Business). However, I recognize we are not debating this topic at the moment; no doubt there will be opportunities to do so.

Mr. Chairman, of course I had a few comments to make on this clause. I think it is a very important clause for us members from Quebec. I am sure the minister is aware of that. Mr. Chairman, I would also like to take this opportunity to note that the minister seemed very relaxed during most part of the evening and the day about the answers he had to give, seemingly finding them very simple. The Quebec government, backed by a unanimous National Assembly, was entirely to blame and its proposition was totally wrong.
Even then, 1 think one must-
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member for Joliette permit me to ask him a question?
He is not honourable.

Someone dared say I am not honourable, so 1 refuse to allow the question, Mr. Chairman.
1 should like to continue my remarks. I know the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) will surely have time to put the questions he must to the Minister of Finance. Anyway, as 1 pointed out a while ago, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Levis went to consult the Minister of Finance. I have a feeling
June 13, 1978

that some arrangement was arrived at on what questions the hon. member for Levis could put and which would perhaps embarrass the Minister of Finance too much. The Minister of Finance would have told him-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member for Joliette says that I go for my information to the Minister of Finance; I feel that is the best place to go for it; he goes for his to the separatist premier of the province of Quebec instead of going to his leader or to the hon. member for York-Simcoe who is the financial critic of his party, unless he was replaced recently.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Levis seems to have been insulted because Premier Levesque did not invite him into his office. I had the great honour, just as the right hon. Prime Minister did of course, of meeting the Quebec premier. Mr. Chairman, for the information of the hon. member for Levis, I should like to add that I told Mr. Levesque that quite a long time had elapsed since 1 had had a cup of coffee with a provincial premier. The last time had been when I had met the late Daniel Johnson, a former premier of the province of Quebec. I do not know why, but some people are blaming me for meeting the Quebec premier, although the right hon. Prime Minister himself has met with all premiers.
He is the Prime Minister.

Our leader has met with all Canadian premiers too. The Minister of Finance gets to meet them from time to time, and we have nothing against that, Mr. Chairman. So 1 wonder why the hon. member for Levis once again criticizes the fact that 1 had the pleasure to meet a man who, whether you like it or not, was legally elected in the province of Quebec in spite, of course, of the efforts made by our friends opposite.
Any way, Mr. Chairman, I would still like to make a brief history of this piece of legislation and of this clause in particular. The Minister of Finance made his comments this afternoon, and 1 remember some of his remarks; he talked about the agreement reached with his provincial counterpart. And there, my question is specifically directed to the Minister of Finance. I do not want to repeat it. The Minister of Finance talked about an agreement with his provincial counterpart, so here is my first question: could the minister explain what kind of agreement was reached with his provincial counterpart and when?
What agreement?

Mr. Chairman, 1 remember and noted immediately that the Minister of Finance talked about an agreement reached with his Quebec provincial counterpart because several members in his party have accused the Minis-
Income Tax Act
ter of Finance of not keeping his word and saying the minister of finance of Quebec had not replied.
I would like to ask him a second question. The Minister of Finance is a man who is surely capable of answering a second question also. I think that in the proposal that was made, in the observations-I do not call that proposals, I call that observations-it seems the minister of finance of Quebec would have hoped for a way of finding a settlement where the federal government could have dealt as between one government and another. And I wonder whether with a little effort at this point the Minister of Finance could tell us if he cannot within the prerogatives that are his come up with a formula which would preserve a very basic principle we have been fighting for for two and half months, a treaty between governments. I imagine the Minister of Finance with the prerogatives his position gives him could come up with something which would be readily acceptable to both sides of the House but would include that basic principle which we and others would also hope for and which Quebec and the National Assembly would accept, I am sure, namely a treaty between one government and another. Could the Minister of Finance clarify that for us?

Mr. Chairman, I cannot help laughing when the hon. member is so convinced about the separatist cause. He is already talking of treaties between two governments in Canada, of agreements between governments. When you talk of treaties, you are talking about two independent countries.
The government concludes agreements with the provinces.
A treaty is between two countries.
Let us say arrangements.

I would not like to give a lecture in international law but a treaty is between two countries. Very well, but that is because the hon. member's thoughts always have strong separatist overtones. Obviously he could not help using those words. Slips of the tongue like this one can happen. It is very simple. I discussed with the provincial ministers about a possible agreement between provincial governments and the federal government relating to the sales tax. All ministers had agreed that they would be in a position to tell me "yes" or "no" when 1 would phone them in the afternoon of budget day just before tabling my budget. When 1 phoned Mr. Parizeau, he said "I'm not saying either yes or no". But all other ministers had answered yes. Then I claimed, and I repeat it, that Mr. Parizeau had broken a gentlemen's agreement. Some will say it is Mr. Parizeau's word against mine. That is correct. But there is circumstancial evidence. Why would the other ministers have taken the responsibility of answering yes on the very day I tabled the budget if there had not been a previous agreement between all of us? It would be easy for me to satisfy

June 13, 1978
Adjournment Debate
any court that there was an agreement between Mr. Parizeau and myself by presenting circumstancial evidence.
He did not say either yes or no.

All the others said yes.

Progress reported.
