subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-REASON FOR BEEF PRICE INCREASES
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-REASON FOR BEEF PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I asked a question of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) about rising beef prices as reflected in retail outlets. I think we all appreciate the difficulties farmers and beef farmers of this country have faced over the last three or four years. In my own community, many farmers have had to sell off their herds simply because they could not make ends meet: there just was not enough revenue to justify the expense of raising cattle.
I do not think any Canadian would object to a 35 per cent or 40 per cent increase in the price of cattle on the hoof. The price of slaughter cows in Winnipeg between early March and June 3 went up 39 per cent. The price of A1 steers increased by 38 per cent. When I see the increase in retail prices, I do not think this is the problem we are facing: I think there is a very important need for stability in the beef market across the country. I think all Canadians, farmers and consumers alike, could do nothing but gain from such stability.
There are some difficulties. The agricultural industry in this country is divided among provincial jurisdictions. The difficulties in bringing these together are very important. I think these difficulties have some effect on stability. However, there is more to it than that. Just doing some comparisons in retail outlets, I found that the price of ground beef went up from 79 cents to roughly $1.39 in about three months, an 87 per cent increase. I mentioned this figure before. But at the same time the price of cows went from $36.15 to $50.25, an increase of only 39 per cent.
I know there are some variations here, but let us look at it in another way. When the slaughter cow price was $36.15 on the Winnipeg market, ground beef cost 79 cents. That was 119 per cent higher than the price on the hoof. Some of this is explained by the fact that there are bones, loss of water, fat, and so forth. However, when the price went to $50.25 on the hoof, the price in the store for ground beef went to $1.39. That is an increase of 178 per cent. Those are the kind of differences we have to examine.

We can go through the same thing with more expensive beef. The price of T-bone steak went from $2.50 to $3.75, while the price of No. 1 steers went from $49.95 to $68.90 on the Winnipeg livestock exchange, an increase in the price of No. 1 steers of 36 per cent and an increase in the price of T-bone steaks of 50 per cent. I recognize that there may be some variations and it is always difficult when we do not have a large research group to do the kind of things we have to do; but I must say I am suspicious of these increases. We are now out of price and wage controls. In a sense, prices were controlled. Certainly, prices at the processing and retail levels were controlled; but prices at the farm gate were not.
Over a period of two or three years several hundred large companies had to turn money back because they made profits in excess of 90 per cent or 95 per cent of their five-year average. With the phasing-out of these controls coming at the same time as the increase in the beef price on the hoof, which 1 think is justified, some things have happened and we should look at them very carefully.
I would like the minister and the government to take a much closer look at this variation, the difference in an increase of, say, 39 per cent and 87 per cent. That is what I am concerned about. I think it should not only concern the consumer; it should concern the farmer; and I am sure it does because in many ways farmers are being blamed. They should not be blamed because they are getting a legitimate increase, yet the consumer is paying what I consider to be close to robbery.

speakeroldname: Mr. Alan G. Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-REASON FOR BEEF PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say at the outset that in a very general sense, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) does, indeed, share the concern of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae). This is one reason why last fall the minister, assisted by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), initiated the three-phase food policy conference program which took place last autumn and winter. This is just a beginning. It is the intention of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, again assisted by the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and others, to move from this base to work toward the further development of a desirable food policy for Canadians which will give consideration to both the production and consumption ends of the scale, bearing in mind the complexities of moving and processing produce from the time it leaves the farm gate to the point at which it may be purchased by consumers at the local level. This is a long-term program.
As I understand the specific situation at hand, there are two main factors behind the recent rapid increase in the price of cheaper beef cuts such as hamburger and blade roast, relative to the more expensive cuts such as T-bone steaks and sirloin steaks. The first, and principal, factor is the natural unfolding of the beef cycle; the second is the current high level of the export of cows to the United States. Let me explain more fully. The beef cycle has two distinct phases: an expansionary phase
June 13, 1978

and a liquidation phase. Over the past few years we have been experiencing the liquidation part of the cycle, not just in Canada but in North America as a whole. This came after a nearly uninterrupted expansion in cattle herds which started away back in the early 1950s. During this time, beef producers expanded cattle herds nearly every year in response to overincreasing consumer demand. Per capita consumption, mainly in beef, doubled over this period from about 50 pounds in 1950 to more than 100 pounds in 1975 and 1976.
The liquidation phase of the beef cycle is characterized by a high level of slaughterings and low prices for caitle and for beef at the retail counter. Also, during this time the supply of beef from which hamburger and blade roasts can be cut is greater than during the expansionary part of the beef cycle. This is because farmers tend to sell off their cows. Thus, the rapid increase in prices for the lower quality cuts relative to the high priced cuts reflects a turning point in the beef cycle: Canada is facing a tight squeeze on its low-grade beef supply and cow marketings are expected to continue to decrease through 1978. The decline of the Canadian dollar relative to the U.S. dollar has aggravated this situation by making it attractive, at times, for American buyers to purchase Canadian cows which could have been slaughtered in Canada.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUESTED INCREASED MILK QUOTAS FOR ONTARIO CHEESE MANUFACTURERS

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUESTED INCREASED MILK QUOTAS FOR ONTARIO CHEESE MANUFACTURERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight on a matter very vital to our national economy and pursuant to my question appearing in Hansard of June 9, 1978, page 6230, as follows:
Following the recent meeting between the Minister of Agriculture and the Ontario minister of agriculture, has a solution been reached to provide increased milk quotas to Ontario cheese manufacturers who are experiencing a serious shortage of milk in their efforts to supply markets waiting for cheese?
The question of the above date and the S.O. 43 motion of May 31, 1978, moved by myself and seconded by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), arise from strong representations made to me and to my party and our agricultural critic, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), and the agricultural committee of the PC party, by the Ontario Cheddar Cheese Association and its member manufacturers regarding the diminishing and inadequate supplies of milk available to the Ontario Cheddar cheese factories.
Also we have received a brief from the Ontario Cheddar Cheese Association, an organization recently formed in that industry. They total at least 32 cheese manufacturing concerns which speak with one voice in the interests of a sound economy for the dairy and cheese producing industries of Ontario. The No. 1 problem in the industrial milk field is the severe shortage of market-sharing quotas for the province of Ontario. This is widely recognized by producer and processor alike. When one couples the MSQ shortage with the specialty cheese market expanding at a high percentage every year, the Ontario Cheddar cheese processor is being placed in an unbearable
Adjournment Debate
situation. Cheddar cheese factories cannot begin to supply the markets which they have developed carefully over long years. Buyers are purchasing a higher percentage of their Cheddar cheese out of the province at the present time.
In 1969, the Murchie-Stewart report advised that several of the smaller plants in Ontario be phased out of operation under the plant consolidation assistance program, and that the remaining plants update their facilities to handle extra milk in a more efficient manner. Most Cheddar factories have spent large sums of money in the past to acquire a greater quota. Now they are faced with the same quota diminishing year after year to the specialty cheese market, at no cost whatsoever to them. The Cheddar processors have virtually no way of expanding their businesses or even holding them at a reasonable level because of this situation. Cheddar plants are running far below their processing capacity during peak milk periods. In the winter months, when monthly percentages go as low as 3 per cent or 4 per cent, this situation becomes critical. The rapidly diminishing milk supply, the variance of monthly milk percentages from a low of 3 per cent or 4 per cent to a high of 14 per cent in May and June, and the fixed overhead costs of these plants place a great deal of the factories in a most undesirable position. Some are facing the prospect of closing their plants for good.
The Ontario Cheddar cheese industry has had a proud and historic record ever since the dairy industry was first instituted in the province. In fact, it was the heart of the dairy industry for a number of years. Ontario has become famous throughout the world for its excellent quality of Cheddar cheese. Now we must ask ourselves whether we will let this great industry wither and die; or will we finally take steps to preserve an industry as much a part of our Ontario heritage as farming itself?
There is one more point I should like to make in the limited time I have. We have a continuing responsibility to see that the Cheddar cheese industry of Ontario obtains its proper and sufficient quota of milk supply. Over the past 20 years, the Canadian government has participated in the amalgamation of cheese factories: it has spent millions of dollars in subsidizing these factories in the succession of amalgamations. Many of the older ones which were obsolete and inefficient, closed. Amalgamation grants were given to the other successor factories which were willing to make improvements and investments in the interest of the economy of the industry. If Ontario's share of the national quota for cheesemaking milk is not increased, we are not supporting past policies; the money put into these amalgamations will go down the drain like so much whey-and perhaps the result will be a bankruptcy of the industry. I, for one, will not stand idly by and see this happen. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) agrees with me.
When I was in Britain a month ago as a delegate to the CPA conference, I asked assembled members of the British Parliament, in a question and answer forum, why our markets

for Canadian cheese in Britain were shrinking so drastically. The answers were not very optimistic: they pointed out that Britain was now a member of the EEC and every country of that common market was a cheese producer to some degree. 1 point out to the minister that in this regard it is our duty to watch every facet of the cheese economy in that every member country of the EEC is subsidized in the products they produce and in the export of those products. We can be-and must be-just as astute.
I am not asking that the Ontario Cheddar Cheese Association be subsidized tonight, tomorrow, or ever. All I am asking is that they be given an ample share of our national milk quota for cheese manufacturing only, to create more production for farmers, to protect the investment and the jobs of the men who make Ontario Cheddar cheese, and to supply the waiting markets with their peerless product.

Yves Caron (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture): Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack), I shall say that the Minister of Agriculture is not responsible for the rules governing the distribution of quotas among the provinces but rather the Canadian supply management committee. This committee is made up of representatives of the governments and the producers of each province under the leadership of the Canadian Dairy Commission.
The control of the industrial milk production in Canada results from a national agreement whereby each province accepted as a basis the percentage of milk which it produced at that time. The same principle applies for eggs, broilers and all other commodities.
As it is a national scheme, there is no evidence that the Canadian consumers do not get the dairy products of the quality and in the quantities they want. So, there is no evidence that Cheddar cheese is scarce at the national level. The supply is adequate.
As for Ontario and specialty cheeses, the Canadian production which stood at 106.1 million pounds in 1974-75 has gone up to 160 million pounds in 1977-78, or increase of 50.8 per cent.
At the same time, in Ontario, the specialty cheese production has gone from 41.2 million pounds to 62.9 million pounds, which represents an increase of 53 per cent, practically the same as the national average.
Given the Ontario production compared with the Canadian production as a whole, it is obvious that the problem experienced by the Cheddar cheese producers is due to the fact that Ontario has reduced the quantities of milk available for this type of dairy product to the benefit of butter producers. It is therefore a problem of milk movement within the province of Ontario itself and consequently it comes under provincial jurisdiction.

The Ontario request for an increase in its marketing quotas is no different from the requests of all the other provinces. Every province from East to West is asking for increased marketing quotas and every Canadian dairy producer wants an increase in his individual marketing quota, and wonders why he does not get it. The answer is quite simple.
The Canadian government has implemented a stable dairy policy and both the producer and the manufacturer are getting a fair return on their investments and their work.

subtopic: CANADIAN CULTURE-IMPORTATION OF U.S. EDITIONS OF CANADIAN BOOKS
CANADIAN CULTURE-IMPORTATION OF U.S. EDITIONS OF CANADIAN BOOKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise tonight in pursuit of a matter that I raised about five times during the earlier part of this session with respect to a very serious problem that faces Canadian publishers and authors, particularly the two dozen or so authors of this country who are successful enough to have their books published abroad, primarily in the United States. It is a problem, really, affecting whether or not we can be masters of our own house with respect to the adequate protection of writers and publishers in this country. I suppose in some ways it is a classic Canadian dilemma, for 1 know of no other country that has so exposed its writers and publishers to the low-cost selling of wholesale editions of works from abroad as we do.
It is not a new problem, Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out the first time 1 raised this matter on November 18, 1977. As far back as 1972 the Ontario royal commission on publishing gave notification that the relevant provision of the Copyright Act was "unworkable in practice and should be reviewed and clarified. We have known of the very serious situation."
Subsequently, since 1975, the government has been notified directly by the Writers Union of Canada, among others, that thousands of dollars in revenue were being lost to publishers and authors and that we were rapidly destroying incentive for major authors to have their works published here. We have made successive representations to this government. I have raised the matter on a number of occasions in this session, but it has been impossible to get action from the government. 1 find this incredible in view of the fact that the basic solutions are not too difficult.
As a solution 1 have suggested repeatedly enforcement of the law through a test case or a specific amendment to the law in instances that would cover, under the Copyright Act, the kind of exposure we are getting today-this kind of threat, the undermining of the publishing industry and the authors of this country. On November 18, 1977, the Secretary of State said there would be clarification of the difficulties in the very near future. On February 27, he said he would "look into it with the
June 13, 1978

utmost dispatch." On June 6, he said they would be making some announcement about this in the very near future.
On other occasions, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) indicated he was also concerned about the problem and would be taking appropriate action. It is quite obvious that he is not prepared to take any action that would involve amendments. As a matter of fact, a fairly straightforward amendment was proposed to the minister by those who represent not only the writers but others involved in his problem, to make the law clear and, in effect, make it say what it is supposed to say and be workable. To this time, the minister-as I understand it-has not taken this matter up with his officials or attempted to draft an amendment. If he has done so, he has not communicated it to this side of the House.
In spite of the offers that have been made informally to pass a specific amendment with dispatch, I do not think any attempt has been made to do so. As far as the powers of seizure by Revenue Canada are concerned, which I believe the minister has indicated might be employed against the sale of remaindered issues, I think it is, at best, an imperfect solution in view of the inevitable and lengthy litigation required before the writers would know if the existing law gives them adequate protection.
We have allowed a situation to develop where the three major book chains in this country, Coles, W.H. Smith and Classic, have opened up the market to the sale of thousands of remaindered editions-American publications of Canadian authors. Initially, only Coles was involved in 1975 when the problem became more acute. By 1977, all three major booksellers who cover a substantial portion of the Canadian market were involved, and virtually nothing has happened.
My specific question tonight relates to the February 27 question I raised in the House, first with the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) and latterly with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I referred to the specific instance of one publication, a book intitled The Book of Eve, by Constance Beresford-Howe, published by MacMillan of Canada and on sale in Montreal and Toronto despite being listed for a year and a half under schedule C in response to complaints by both the author and the publisher. Counsel for both Revenue Canada and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs stated they will not take action because they claim schedule C does not specifically encompass books.
In earlier discussions, the Secretary of State and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said they might develop a mechanism that would reduce the effective notification period from something like six months to one month. On February 27, the Secretary of State said, "I will look into it with the utmost dispatch." If that is the kind of utmost dispatch we get from the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) or from any other minister of the government, these poor authors and publishers will have to wait a mighty long time. The early expression of pious hope or the use of moral suasion on the

three major Canadian book chains seem, to me, to have been abandoned by this government. As yet it appears that we have received no substantial indication of action. I would hope that tonight the parliamentary secretary can give us an indication of clearcut leadership that will now be taken on this very important problem.

Mr. Speaker, the minister and his officials are well aware of the position advanced by the Writers Union of Canada concerning remainders. What appears on the surface to be a simple, direct problem capable of rapid solution is, however, far more complex than would appear to the hon. member's eye. The writers have available to them the normal civil processes available in all forms of intellectual property law. For a multitude of reasons, they have not fully exploited the benefits available to them under these provisions.
If the government were able and decided to enter directly into litigation, the long-term consequences could be significant indeed. Officials of the department, in conjunction with officials of the Departments of Justice and National Revenue, have been attempting to find a solution to the problem that would permit a judicial review of the existing legislation and, at the same time, relieve the potential financial liability writers would face in bringing the matter to trial. I am pleased to say that we are now close to the solution and in a few days it may be possible to make an announcement to that effect.
One proposal put forth by the Writers Union, and supported in a statement by the hon. member, is for a quick and simple amendment to the existing statute. The minister has considered this and is reluctant to proceed on the matter. In part, this reluctance stems from the fact that the entire copyright law is undergoing comprehensive review which has recently generated more than 90 briefs on proposals made to the government last year. If the government were to make an exception for the Writers Union in this case, it would quickly be inundated with requests for special treatment in a myriad other cases. The benefits of a general and comprehensive review would be lost and the consequences to the long-term welfare of both creators and users of copyright material would be significant indeed.
A careful reading of the proposed amendment mentioned by the hon. member in an earlier communication to the minister raises some doubt as to the central purpose of the amendment. It would appear, to some at least, that the change would not only exclude remainders but the importation of any foreign editions of Canadian authors whether or not they were available in Canada. If this is, indeed, one of the possible outcomes, then Canadian readers and buyers of books could possibly experience a substantial increase in book prices and Canadian authors might expect a decline in sales since there are few, if any, products whose sales are immune to substantial price increases.
